verse.text: In the beginning was the Logos, and the Logos was with God, and the Logos was God.
verse.note: Greek logos means word, speech, message or reason. Nearly all translations render it 'Word', and most scholars see John's main background in the Hebrew Bible: God creating by speaking in Genesis 1, 'the word of the Lord', and the figure of Wisdom, which 'Word' reflects and 'Logos' does not. Greek-speaking readers would also have heard the philosophical sense of logos as the reason that orders the world. The Greek term is kept here as a title because 'the Word' is now commonly taken to mean the Bible, which is not what John means.

In the Greek, 'God' in this clause has no article and stands first as the predicate, so the clause says what the Logos was and does not simply equate him with the one he was 'with'. Some render it 'what God was, the Logos was'. The mainstream view is that the wording ascribes full deity to the Logos while distinguishing him from the Father; the rendering 'a god' is rejected by most grammarians.

verse.text: He was in the beginning with God.
All things came into being through him, and apart from him not one thing came into being. What has come into being

note.traditional: without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, and these words can either end the previous sentence ('not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life') or begin the next, as here. The SBLGNT and most early Christian writers take them with what follows; many English translations take them with what precedes. On the reading adopted, the sense may also be 'What has come into being was life in him.'

verse.text: in him was life, and the life was the light of humanity.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to seize or take hold of, and so either to overpower or to grasp with the mind. Older translations have 'comprehended'; most modern ones have 'overcome', which suits the image of darkness and light. John may intend both senses.

verse.text: There came a man sent from God, whose name was John.
He came for testimony, to testify about the light, so that all might believe through him.
He was not the light, but came to testify about the light.
The true light, which gives light to every person, was coming into the world.

note.traditional: which lighteth every man that cometh into the world

verse.note: 'Coming into the world' can describe the light, as here, or 'every person' ('which gives light to every person who comes into the world'). Most modern translations and commentators take it of the light, since John elsewhere speaks of Jesus as coming into the world.

verse.text: He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him.
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not receive him.
But to all who did receive him, he gave the right to become children of God—to those who believe in his name,
who were born not from blood, nor from the will of flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God.
And the Logos became flesh and made his dwelling among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
verse.note: The Greek verb is related to the word for a tent and for the tabernacle, the tent in which God's presence lived among Israel in the wilderness. The mention of 'glory' that follows strengthens the echo, since God's glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). Many scholars think the allusion is deliberate.

The Greek word means the only one of its kind and was regularly used of an only child; 'Son' is supplied here from that sense. The traditional 'only begotten' assumes a link with the verb 'beget', but the second half of the word is related to 'kind'. 'One and only' or 'only' is the mainstream modern rendering, though a minority of scholars have recently defended 'only begotten'.

verse.text: (John testifies about him and has cried out, saying, “This was the one of whom I said, ‘The one coming after me has come to rank ahead of me, because he was before me.’”)
For from his fullness we have all received, grace in place of grace.

note.traditional: grace upon grace; grace for grace

verse.note: The Greek preposition normally means 'in place of' or 'in exchange for', and the sense 'upon', as in the familiar 'grace upon grace', is hard to document elsewhere. On the rendering here, one gift of grace succeeds another, which the next verse may explain: the law given through Moses, then grace and truth through Jesus Christ. Many scholars still prefer 'grace upon grace', meaning grace in unbroken supply, and the question remains open.

verse.text: For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
No one has ever seen God. The one and only, himself God, who is at the Father’s side—he has made him known.

note.term: The one and only, himself God

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'one and only God'; the majority of later manuscripts read 'the one and only Son'. Most textual critics judge 'God' original as the older and more difficult reading, and the SBLGNT prints it. The rendering here takes 'God' as a second description of the one and only, not as a reference to a second God.

verse.text: And this is John’s testimony, when the Jewish leaders sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'the Jews', but everyone in this scene, John included, is Jewish; the group that sends priests and Levites from Jerusalem is the authorities there. John's Gospel often uses the word in this narrower way. Scholars are divided over how to translate it: some argue for 'Judeans' throughout, while others object that this removes Jews from the New Testament.

verse.text: He declared openly and did not deny it; he declared, “I am not the Messiah.”
verse.note: Greek christos, 'anointed one', translates the Hebrew title that gives English 'Messiah', the anointed king Israel expected. Where it is a title under discussion, as here, this translation uses 'Messiah'; where it is attached to Jesus's name, as in verse 17, it keeps 'Christ'. Several modern translations make the same division. In verse 41 John himself gives the Semitic form of the title and explains it with the Greek one.

verse.text: And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”
verse.note: Two expected figures are in view. Malachi 4:5 promised that Elijah would return before the day of the Lord, and Deuteronomy 18:15–18 promised a prophet like Moses, whom many came to expect as a figure of the last days. John refuses these titles along with that of Messiah.

verse.text: So they said to him, “Who are you? We must give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”
He said, “I am a voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.”
Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.
They questioned him and said to him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”
John answered them, “I baptize in water. Among you stands one whom you do not know,
verse.note: Most translations have 'with water'. The Greek preposition most naturally means 'in', and the verb in ordinary usage meant to dip or immerse, so 'in water' is probably what a Greek reader heard; 'with' is also grammatically possible. The same construction is rendered 'in the Holy Spirit' in verse 33.

text.q: the one coming after me; I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.”

verse.text: These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!

text.q: This is the one about whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who has come to rank ahead of me, because he was before me.’
I myself did not know him, but I came baptizing in water for this reason: that he might be revealed to Israel.”

verse.text: And John testified, “I have seen the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and remain on him.

text.q: I myself did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘The one on whom you see the Spirit come down and remain, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’
And I have seen, and I have testified that this is the Chosen One of God.”

verse.note: Most manuscripts, including most of the early ones, read 'the Son of God', and most translations follow them. A few early witnesses read 'the Chosen One of God', which the SBLGNT prints on the argument that scribes were more likely to change an unusual title into the familiar one than the reverse. The question remains disputed.

verse.text: The next day John was again standing there with two of his disciples,
and looking at Jesus as he walked by, he said, “Look, the Lamb of God!”
The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which, translated, means Teacher), “where are you staying?”
He said to them, “Come and you will see.” So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.
verse.note: Hours were normally counted from sunrise, so the tenth hour is about four in the afternoon. A minority view holds that John counts from midnight, which would make it ten in the morning.

verse.text: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard John and followed Jesus.
He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which is translated Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon, son of John. You will be called Cephas” (which is translated Peter).
The next day Jesus decided to leave for Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found the one Moses wrote about in the law, and the prophets too: Jesus son of Joseph, from Nazareth.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said about him, “Look, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit!”
Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, while you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”
Jesus answered him, “Do you believe because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.”
And he said to him, “Truly, truly I tell you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God going up and coming down on the Son of Man.”

note.term: going up and coming down on the Son of Man
note.traditional: ascending and descending upon the Son of man

verse.note: The picture comes from Jacob's dream in Genesis 28:12, in which angels go up and down a stairway between earth and heaven; Jesus puts himself in the stairway's place. It follows naturally on verse 47, since Jacob, later renamed Israel, was known for his deceit (Genesis 27:35). 'You' in this sentence is plural: Jesus is now addressing more than Nathanael.

verse.text: On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus’s mother was there.
Jesus and his disciples had also been invited to the wedding.
When the wine ran out, Jesus’s mother said to him, “They have no wine.”
Jesus said to her, “What does this have to do with me, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

note.term: What does this have to do with me
note.traditional: What have I to do with thee?

verse.note: The Greek is a compressed idiom, literally “What to me and to you?”, familiar from the Greek Old Testament. It usually puts distance between speaker and hearer: “Why are you involving me?” Some translators instead take it as “What concern is that to you and to me?”, which makes the shortage neither person’s business. In both readings Jesus declines to act at once without rebuking her.

In Greek this was an ordinary and courteous way to address a woman, without the harshness the bare word has in modern English. Jesus uses it again to his mother from the cross (19:26). It is nonetheless an unusual way for a son to address his mother, and many interpreters think it signals some distance. No English term captures both the courtesy and the reserve, so the plain word is kept.

verse.text: His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
Now six stone water jars were standing there for the purification rites of the Jews, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.

note.traditional: two or three firkins / twenty or thirty gallons

verse.note: The Greek says each jar held “two or three measures”. The measure in question was a liquid unit of roughly 39 litres, or about nine to ten gallons. The six jars together held somewhere around 120 to 180 gallons (about 450 to 700 litres). Stone vessels were preferred for purification water because, in Jewish practice, stone was not considered liable to ritual impurity.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them to the brim.
Then he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet.” So they took it.

note.traditional: governor of the feast / master of the feast

verse.note: The Greek word is rare. It may mean the head servant in charge of the dining arrangements, or a guest chosen to preside over the feast. His free manner with the bridegroom in verse 10 fits a presiding guest somewhat better, but the matter is not settled. “Master of the banquet” leaves both possibilities open.

verse.text: When the master of the banquet tasted the water that had become wine—he did not know where it came from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew—he called the bridegroom
and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and the lesser wine once the guests are drunk. You have kept the good wine until now.”

note.traditional: have well drunk / have drunk freely

verse.note: The verb means to become intoxicated, and that is its regular sense in the period. Many English versions soften it to “have drunk freely”. The man is quoting a general rule of thumb about hosts and is not describing the state of these particular guests. The Greek says simply “when they are drunk”; “the guests” is supplied for clarity.

verse.text: Jesus did this as the beginning of his signs in Cana of Galilee; he revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him.
After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days.
The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
In the temple courts he found people selling cattle, sheep and doves, and the money changers sitting at their tables.
verse.note: John uses two different words that English versions usually both translate “temple”. The word here means the whole sacred complex with its outer courts, where the trading took place. The word in verses 19–21 means the sanctuary building itself. “Temple courts” here and “temple” there keeps the distinction a Greek reader would have heard.

verse.text: He made a whip out of cords and drove them all out of the temple courts, sheep and cattle alike; he poured out the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables,

note.traditional: drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen

verse.note: The Greek can mean that Jesus drove out all the animals (“all of them, both the sheep and the cattle”), or that he drove out all the traders together with their animals. The grammar slightly favours the first reading, but “all” is masculine and could refer to the people. The rendering follows the first reading and leaves the second possible.

verse.text: and to those selling the doves he said, “Take these out of here! Stop making my Father’s house a house of trade.”
His disciples remembered that it is written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”

note.term: Zeal for your house will consume me.
note.traditional: The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up

verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 69:9 (68:10 in the Greek numbering), a psalm of a righteous sufferer that early Christians often applied to Jesus. The psalm has “has consumed me”; John’s wording has the future “will consume”, which readers have long taken as pointing forward to Jesus’s death.

verse.text: So the Jewish leaders responded and said to him, “What sign do you show us, since you are doing these things?”
verse.note: The Greek says simply “the Jews”, as in verses 6 and 13. Here and in verse 20 those who demand Jesus’s credentials for acting in the temple are best understood as the authorities responsible for it, not the Jewish people as a whole, to whom Jesus and his disciples belonged. John often uses the term in this narrower way. Scholars are divided on how to translate it: some prefer “Judeans” throughout, while others keep “the Jews” everywhere.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it.”
The Jewish leaders then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and you will raise it in three days?”

note.traditional: Forty and six years was this temple in building

verse.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the Jerusalem temple around 20–19 BC, which places this exchange at about AD 27–28. Work on the wider complex continued until the 60s AD, only a few years before the Romans destroyed it. The Greek could describe a completed phase of building or construction still in progress.

verse.text: But he was speaking about the temple of his body.
So when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
While he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the festival, many trusted in his name, seeing the signs he was doing.
verse.note: The same Greek verb appears in verse 23 and verse 24: many “trusted” in Jesus, but Jesus did not “trust” himself to them. Traditional versions have “believed” and then “commit” or “entrust”, which hides the deliberate echo. The verb covers both believing and trusting; it is rendered “believed” in verses 11 and 22 and “trusted” here so that the echo can be heard.

verse.text: But Jesus, for his part, did not trust himself to them, because he knew everyone
and because he had no need for anyone to testify about a person, for he himself knew what was in a person.
Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.
He came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”
Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.”
verse.note: The Greek adverb can mean either 'from above' or 'again', and the conversation turns on that double sense: Nicodemus hears 'a second time' (verse 4), while Jesus goes on to speak of birth from the Spirit. Elsewhere in John, including verse 31 of this chapter, the word means 'from above', so that sense is given in the text. Many translations keep 'born again' and footnote the alternative; scholars widely agree that both meanings are in play and that no single English word carries both.

verse.text: Nicodemus said to him, “How can a person be born when he is an old man? He cannot enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born, can he?”
Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of God.

text.q: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Do not be amazed that I said to you, ‘You must all be born from above.’

note.term: You must all be born from above

verse.note: Greek distinguishes singular and plural 'you'. Jesus addresses Nicodemus in the singular, but here he switches to the plural, and the 'you' in 'you do not accept' (verse 11) and throughout verse 12 is plural as well. Nicodemus, who began with 'we know' in verse 2, is being addressed as the representative of a wider group.

text.q: The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

note.term: The wind blows where it wishes
note.traditional: The wind blows where it wishes

verse.note: One Greek word means 'wind', 'breath' and 'spirit', and the word translated 'sound' also means 'voice'. The sentence can therefore also be heard as 'The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice'; the comparison works in Greek because the same word serves for both. Like most translations, this one gives 'wind' here and 'Spirit' at the end of the verse.

verse.text: Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things happen?”
Jesus answered him, “You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not understand these things?

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen, yet you do not accept our testimony.
If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?
No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.
And just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,

verse.note: The reference is to Numbers 21:4-9, where Moses set a bronze snake on a pole and those bitten by snakes lived when they looked at it. The Greek verb means both to raise something physically and to exalt. John uses it of Jesus being raised on the cross (see 12:32-33), and most interpreters think the sense of exaltation is intended as well.

text.q: so that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.”

verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage of the period 'eternal life' meant the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In John this life is spoken of as something the believer already has (see verse 36).

note.term: may have eternal life in him
note.traditional: whoever believes in him may have eternal life

verse.note: The words 'in him' can be taken with 'believes' or with 'have eternal life'. John's regular expression for believing in someone uses a different preposition, as in verse 16, which favours the second reading adopted here. Many translations take the first, and some manuscripts have John's usual preposition, with a number also adding 'may not perish' from verse 16.

verse.text: For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

note.term: For God so loved the world

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts have no quotation marks, and it is unclear where Jesus's words to Nicodemus end. This translation closes the speech at verse 15 and treats verses 16-21 as the evangelist's own reflection, because of the shift to past tenses and to phrasing that elsewhere belongs to the narrator. Many translations and red-letter editions continue Jesus's speech through verse 21, and scholars are divided.

The Greek adverb normally means 'in this way', but paired with the following 'that' it can also express degree, 'so much'. The traditional 'so loved' is kept because, like the Greek, it can be heard either way. Some scholars argue for 'this is how God loved the world: he gave', while the majority of translations understand 'loved so much that he gave'.

The Greek word means 'the only one of its kind' and was used of an only child; its second half is related to 'kind', not to 'beget'. 'One and only' or 'only' is the usual modern rendering. A minority of scholars have recently defended the older 'only begotten'.

verse.text: For God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.
verse.note: Most English translations have 'condemn' in verses 17 and 18 and then 'judgment' or 'verdict' in verse 19, though some keep 'judge' throughout. The Greek uses the ordinary verb for judging and its related noun across all three verses; the context shows that an adverse judgment is meant. 'Judge' is kept so that the connection is visible, both here and with later passages in John where judgment is discussed.

verse.text: Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because they have not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.
And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light, because their deeds were evil.
For everyone who practices what is base hates the light and does not come to the light, so that their deeds may not be exposed.
But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be shown that their deeds have been done in God.
After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and there he spent time with them and was baptizing.
John too was baptizing, at Aenon near Salim, because there was plenty of water there, and people were coming and being baptized;
for John had not yet been thrown into prison.
Then a dispute arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew about purification.
They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, the one you have testified about—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him.”
John answered, “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it has been given to him from heaven.

text.q: You yourselves testify for me that I said, ‘I am not the Messiah,’ but, ‘I have been sent ahead of him.’

verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew for 'anointed one', the king Israel was expecting. Here John is denying a title, not using a name, so 'Messiah' is used; where the word functions as part of Jesus's name, this translation keeps 'Christ'. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and listens to him, is overjoyed at the bridegroom’s voice. So this joy of mine is now complete.
He must increase, but I must decrease.”

verse.text: The one who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. The one who comes from heaven is above all.

note.term: The one who comes from above is above all

verse.note: It is unclear whether verses 31-36 continue John the Baptist's speech or are the evangelist's comment. They are treated here as the evangelist's words, since they echo the language of the conversation with Nicodemus and of verses 16-21. Some translations keep the quotation open to the end of the chapter, and the question is disputed.

verse.text: He testifies to what he has seen and heard, yet no one accepts his testimony.
Whoever has accepted his testimony has set their seal to this: God is true.
For the one whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.

note.term: he gives the Spirit without measure
note.traditional: God gives the Spirit without measure

verse.note: The Greek does not state the subject of 'gives'. Most interpreters understand that God gives the Spirit without limit to the one he has sent, and some manuscripts add 'God' to make this explicit. It is also possible to read it as the one sent giving the Spirit without limit; the translation leaves 'he' as open as the Greek.

verse.text: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever disobeys the Son will not see life; instead, the wrath of God remains on them.
Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—
though in fact Jesus himself was not baptizing; his disciples were—
he left Judea and went away again to Galilee.
And he had to pass through Samaria.
So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of land that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.
Jacob’s spring was there. So Jesus, tired out from the journey, sat down just as he was beside the spring. It was about the sixth hour.
verse.note: The narrator and Jesus use the word for a spring or source (here and in verse 14), while the woman uses a different word meaning a dug well (verses 11–12). Most translations say “well” throughout. Keeping the two words apart lets the reader hear the link between Jacob’s spring and the “spring of water welling up” that Jesus promises.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon, the hottest part of the day; the seventh hour in verse 52 is about one in the afternoon. A minority of scholars think John counts from midnight, but most do not accept this.

verse.text: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone away into the town to buy food.
So the Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.
verse.note: The verb can mean to associate on friendly terms or, more narrowly, to use something together with someone. On the second reading the point is that Jews would not share a drinking vessel with Samaritans for reasons of purity, which fits the scene well. The sentence is the narrator’s explanation, and a few early manuscripts lack it.

verse.text: Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
verse.note: In ordinary usage, including the Greek Old Testament, “living water” meant fresh, flowing water from a spring or stream as opposed to still water in a cistern. The woman takes Jesus in this everyday sense, which is why she asks where he will get it without a bucket. Jesus means water that gives life.

verse.text: The woman said to him, “Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep. Where then do you get this living water?

text.q: Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?”

verse.text: Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again,

text.q: but whoever drinks the water that I will give them will never be thirsty again. Instead, the water that I will give them will become in them a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”

verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come. It describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

verse.text: The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or keep coming all the way here to draw.”
He said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come back here.”
The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right to say, ‘I have no husband,’

text.q: for you have had five husbands, and the man you have now is not your husband. In this you have spoken the truth.”

verse.text: The woman said to him, “Sir, I see that you are a prophet.

text.q: Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you people say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.”

verse.note: The mountain is Gerizim, which rises above the site and was the holy place of the Samaritans. Their temple there had been destroyed by the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus in the late second century BC, but they continued to worship on the mountain. Where God was to be worshiped was the central dispute between Samaritans and Jews.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “Believe me, woman, an hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.

text.q: You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews.
But an hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking just such people to worship him.

verse.note: Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so “spirit” here may be the human spirit, meaning inward and genuine worship, or God’s Spirit, meaning worship made possible by the Spirit whom Jesus gives. Many interpreters of John favor the second, given how the Gospel speaks of the Spirit elsewhere. The lower-case rendering leaves the question open.

text.q: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

verse.text: The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming,” the one called Christ. “When he comes, he will tell us everything.”
verse.note: “Messiah” here is a Greek spelling of the Hebrew and Aramaic word for “anointed one,” and “Christ” is its Greek translation. The explanation is probably the narrator’s aside for Greek readers, as at 1:41, though it could be read as part of the woman’s speech. Samaritans did not use the title Messiah, as far as is known, but expected a prophet like Moses who would restore and reveal all things.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one speaking to you.”

note.traditional: I that speak unto thee am he

verse.note: The Greek is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.” In context it is the ordinary way of saying “I am he,” that is, the Messiah she has just mentioned. Many scholars also hear in it the first of John’s absolute “I am” sayings, which echo God’s self-declarations in Isaiah.

verse.text: Just then his disciples came, and they were amazed that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said, “What do you want?” or, “Why are you speaking with her?”
So the woman left her water jar and went away into the town and said to the people,

text.q: “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did! Could this be the Messiah?”

verse.note: The Greek word is the one translated “Christ” in verse 25. Here it is a title under discussion, not a name, and a first-century hearer would have heard the role of the expected anointed deliverer, which “Messiah” conveys to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. The form of the woman’s question in Greek is tentative, neither a confident claim nor a denial.

verse.text: They went out of the town and were coming to him.
Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, “Rabbi, eat.”
But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”
So the disciples said to one another, “Surely no one has brought him something to eat?”
Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to complete his work.

text.q: Do you not say, ‘Four months more, and then the harvest comes’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes and see the fields: they are white for harvest. Already

verse.note: The word “already” stands at the boundary between two sentences and can go with either. Older translations attach it to what precedes: the fields are “already white for harvest.” The Greek edition followed here, with many modern translations, takes it with what follows: the reaper is already receiving wages.

text.q: the reaper is receiving wages and gathering a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together.
For in this the saying is true: ‘One sows and another reaps.’
I sent you to reap what you have not labored for. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”

verse.text: Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything I did.”
So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
And many more believed because of his word,
and they said to the woman, “We no longer believe because of what you said, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.”
After the two days he left there for Galilee.
For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.
verse.note: The word can mean a homeland or a hometown, and it is disputed which place John means. If it is Galilee, the welcome in verse 45 is shallow, resting only on the signs people had seen. If it is Judea or Jerusalem, the saying explains why Jesus left there. Interpreters remain divided.

verse.text: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen everything he had done in Jerusalem at the festival, for they too had gone to the festival.
So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. Now there was a certain royal official whose son was sick in Capernaum.
verse.note: The word means someone attached to a king, whether a courtier, an officer, or a member of the royal household. In Galilee this would be a man in the service of Herod Antipas, the ruler of the region, who was popularly called king. Whether the man was Jewish or a Gentile is not stated.

verse.text: When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and begged him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
So Jesus said to him, “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.”
The official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”
Jesus said to him, “Go; your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.
He was already on his way down when his slaves met him and told him that his boy was alive.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes people owned by a master, not hired staff. “Servants” is the traditional English rendering, but it suggests free employees to a modern reader. Slaves in a wealthy household could hold responsible positions, yet they remained their master’s property.

verse.text: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they told him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”
So the father realized that it was at that very hour that Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives.” And he believed, he and his whole household.
This was now the second sign that Jesus performed after coming from Judea to Galilee.
After this there was a festival of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now there is in Jerusalem, by the Sheep Gate, a pool called in Hebrew Bethesda, which has five colonnades.

note.traditional: by the sheep gate (older versions: by the sheep market)

verse.note: The Greek has only an adjective, “the sheep-something,” and leaves the noun to be supplied. Most translations supply “gate,” since Nehemiah mentions a Sheep Gate in Jerusalem’s wall. The sentence can also be read as “by the Sheep Pool there is a place called Bethesda.”

The manuscripts disagree on the name: some read Bethzatha, others Bethsaida, and there are further spellings. The SBLGNT text prints Bethesda, the familiar form, though editors are divided. “In Hebrew” here includes Aramaic, the everyday Semitic language of the region, which Greek writers did not usually distinguish from Hebrew.

verse.text: In these lay a crowd of the sick: blind, lame, and withered.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts continue with “waiting for the movement of the water” and add a verse 4, which says that an angel went down into the pool from time to time and stirred the water, and that the first person in afterward was healed. The earliest manuscripts lack these words, and the Greek text translated here omits them, which is why the numbering passes from 3 to 5. The addition was probably made to explain the sick man’s remark in verse 7.

verse.text: A certain man was there who had been ill for thirty-eight years.
When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been that way a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to become well?”
The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up; and while I am on my way, someone else goes down ahead of me.”
Jesus said to him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.”
And at once the man became well, and he picked up his mat and began to walk. Now that day was a Sabbath.
So the Jewish leaders said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and you are not permitted to pick up your mat.”
verse.note: The Greek says simply “the Jews,” but in this scene John uses the term for the authorities in Jerusalem who police Sabbath observance, not for the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus and the healed man are Jews too. The narrower rendering is used in verses 10–18 to make that clear. Scholars are divided on how to translate the word in John: some prefer “Judeans” throughout, others keep “Jews” everywhere.

Carrying a load on the Sabbath was treated as forbidden work, on the basis of passages such as Jeremiah 17:21–22, and later rabbinic law lists carrying an object from one place to another among the prohibited kinds of labor. The objection is to the man carrying his bedding, not at first to the healing itself.

verse.text: But he answered them, “The one who made me well, he is the one who said to me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’”
They asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ‘Pick it up and walk’?”
But the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had slipped away, since there was a crowd in the place.
After this Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you have become well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.”
The man went away and told the Jewish leaders that it was Jesus who had made him well.
And for this reason the Jewish leaders began to persecute Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.
But he answered them, “My Father has been working until now, and I am working too.”

note.term: My Father has been working until now

verse.note: Genesis says God rested on the seventh day, yet Jewish interpreters of the period commonly held that God never stops sustaining the world, giving life and judging, even on the Sabbath. Jesus claims the same exemption for himself, which is why the next verse says his hearers took him to be making himself equal to God.

verse.text: For this reason, then, the Jewish leaders were seeking all the more to kill him, because he was not only breaking the Sabbath but was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God.

So Jesus answered and said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, the Son also does in the same way.

text.q: For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself is doing, and he will show him greater works than these, so that you will be amazed.
For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those he wishes.
Nor does the Father judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the Son,
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears my word and believes the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has crossed over from death into life.

verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. John’s striking point here is that the believer already has it. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.
For just as the Father has life in himself, so also he has given the Son to have life in himself;
and he has given him authority to carry out judgment, because he is the Son of Man.

verse.note: Here alone in the Gospels the phrase lacks the Greek definite article. Most interpreters take it as the title all the same, since Greek often drops the article in this construction, and the wording echoes Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a son of man” is given authority. Others read “because he is a son of man,” that is, a human being, so that humanity is judged by one of its own.

text.q: Do not be amazed at this, for an hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice
and will come out: those who have done good to a resurrection of life, and those who have practiced evil to a resurrection of judgment.
I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will but the will of the one who sent me.
If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true.

verse.note: The point is legal, not a concession that Jesus might be lying. In Jewish law, as in ancient courts generally, a person’s unsupported testimony on his own behalf did not count, and a matter had to be established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus therefore goes on to call witnesses: John, his own works, the Father and the Scriptures.

text.q: There is another who testifies about me, and I know that the testimony he gives about me is true.
You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth.
But I do not accept testimony from a human being; rather, I say these things so that you may be saved.
He was the lamp that burns and shines, and you were willing for a time to rejoice in his light.
But I have testimony greater than John’s. For the works that the Father has given me to complete, the very works that I am doing, testify about me that the Father has sent me,
and the Father who sent me has himself testified about me. You have never heard his voice or seen his form,
and you do not have his word remaining in you, because you do not believe the one he sent.
You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that testify about me,

verse.note: The Greek verb form can be either a statement (“you search”) or a command (“search!”). Older English versions took it as a command; most modern translations and commentators read a statement, because the following words, “because you think … yet you are not willing,” describe what the hearers already do.

text.q: yet you are not willing to come to me so that you may have life.
I do not accept glory from people,
but I know you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves.

verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean love for God or God’s own love. Most interpreters take it here as love for God, which the hearers lack, but the other sense is possible, and the English phrase leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

text.q: I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not accept me; if another comes in his own name, him you will accept.
How can you believe, when you accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?
Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. The one who accuses you is Moses, in whom you have set your hope.
For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.
But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

verse.text: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, that is, of Tiberias.
A large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs he was performing on the sick.
Jesus went up the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.
Now the Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near.
So when Jesus looked up and saw that a large crowd was coming toward him, he said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread so that these people may eat?”
He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.
Philip answered him, “Bread worth two hundred denarii would not be enough for each of them to get even a little.”

note.traditional: two hundred denarii; two hundred pennyworth; half a year’s wages

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a hired labourer. Two hundred denarii was therefore well over half a year’s wages, which is the point of Philip’s reply.

verse.text: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,

text.q: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are these among so many?”

verse.text: Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was plenty of grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.
Then Jesus took the loaves, and after giving thanks he distributed them to those who were seated, and likewise of the fish, as much as they wanted.
When they were full, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the leftover pieces, so that nothing is lost.”
So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with pieces of the five barley loaves that were left over by those who had eaten.
When the people saw the sign he had performed, they began to say, “This truly is the Prophet who is to come into the world.”
verse.note: The crowd is not calling Jesus one prophet among many. They identify him with the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18, a figure many expected in the last days. A feeding in a remote place near Passover would naturally recall Moses and the manna, and the move to make Jesus king in the next verse follows from that expectation.

verse.text: So Jesus, knowing that they were about to come and seize him to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,
got into a boat, and started across the sea toward Capernaum. It had already grown dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them,
and the sea was being stirred up by a strong wind that was blowing.
When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were afraid.
verse.note: A stadion was a Greek measure of about 185 metres, so twenty-five or thirty stadia is roughly three to three and a half miles (about five kilometres). The lake is about seven miles across at its widest, so the disciples were well out from shore.

verse.text: But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “I am”, which is the ordinary way to say “It’s me”, and that is the plain sense here. The same two words open “I am the bread of life” in verse 35 and stand alone at John 8:58, and in the Greek Old Testament they are used for God’s self-declaration (for example Isaiah 43:10). Many interpreters think John intends that echo in this scene of mastery over the sea, but this cannot be proved from the phrase alone.

verse.text: Then they wanted to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land they were heading for.

The next day the crowd that had stayed on the other side of the sea saw that there had been no other boat there, only the one, and that Jesus had not boarded the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.
But boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats themselves and went to Capernaum, looking for Jesus.
When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you get here?”
Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you are looking for me not because you saw signs but because you ate of the loaves and were satisfied.

text.q: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for on him the Father, God, has set his seal.”

verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age”. In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In John this life is something the believer already has (verses 47 and 54) and not only a future hope.

verse.text: Then they said to him, “What are we to do, to work the works of God?”
Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God: that you believe in the one he sent.”
So they said to him, “Then what sign do you perform, so that we may see it and believe you? What work do you do?

text.q: Our ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”

note.term: He gave them bread from heaven to eat
note.traditional: He gave them bread from heaven to eat

verse.note: The wording is closest to Psalm 78:24, with echoes of Exodus 16:4 and 16:15. The crowd is challenging Jesus to match Moses, and some Jewish writings from around this period expected manna to be given again in the age to come. The rest of the discourse is in effect an exposition of this quotation.

verse.text: Then Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it is not Moses who has given you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.

text.q: For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”

note.term: that which comes down from heaven
note.traditional: he who comes down from heaven; that which comes down from heaven

verse.note: The Greek can mean either “that which comes down” (the bread) or “he who comes down” (a person), because “bread” is grammatically masculine. The crowd takes it in the first sense, as their request in verse 34 shows, and the translation follows them. Jesus makes the personal sense explicit in verse 35, and the double meaning is probably deliberate.

verse.text: So they said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”
Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.

text.q: But I told you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.
Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never throw out,
because I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of the one who sent me.
And this is the will of the one who sent me: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.
For this is the will of my Father: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day.”

verse.text: Then the Jews began to grumble about him because he had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven,”
verse.note: This verb and its close relatives are what the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel’s grumbling against Moses in the wilderness, including in the manna story (Exodus 16–17; Numbers 14). A reader who knew those Scriptures would hear the echo: the hearers who appeal to the manna are behaving like the generation that ate it.

verse.text: and they said, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How can he now say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?”
Jesus answered them, “Stop grumbling among yourselves.

text.q: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws them, and I will raise them up on the last day.
It is written in the prophets: ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.
Not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes has eternal life.
I am the bread of life.
Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.
This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that a person may eat of it and not die.
I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, they will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.”

verse.text: Then the Jews began to quarrel with one another, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”
So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves.

text.q: Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day.

verse.note: From this verse to verse 58 the Greek uses a different verb for eating from the one in verses 49–53. In older Greek it meant to gnaw or munch, and some interpreters think John chose it to make the language more graphic. Others point out that John uses it as his ordinary present-tense verb for “eat” (also at 13:18), so that no change of meaning is intended. The translation follows the second view; the question is disputed.

text.q: For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.
Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in them.
Just as the living Father sent me and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.
This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like what the ancestors ate, and they died. Whoever eats this bread will live forever.”

verse.text: He said these things while teaching in the synagogue in Capernaum.
Many of his disciples, when they heard it, said, “This is a harsh saying. Who can listen to it?”
verse.note: The Greek word means hard in the sense of rough, harsh or unpleasant, not hard to understand. The disciples’ complaint is that what Jesus has said is objectionable, and “hard” in modern English suggests it was merely puzzling. Most translations keep “hard”; some use “difficult”. The final words could also be read “Who can listen to him?”

verse.text: But Jesus, knowing within himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Does this make you stumble?
verse.note: The verb means to trip someone up, to cause them to fall, and in the New Testament usually to fall away from faith. “Offend” was accurate in older English but now suggests hurt feelings. The stronger sense fits the context, since in verse 66 many disciples do turn back. Some recent translations render it similarly, with “cause to stumble” or “take offense”.

text.q: Then what if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?
It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life.

verse.text: But there are some among you who do not believe.” For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would hand him over.
verse.note: The verb means to hand over or deliver up. The New Testament uses the same word for the leaders handing Jesus to Pilate and Pilate handing him over to be crucified. Greek has a separate word for betrayal, which is not used here. Most translations render “betray” when Judas is the subject, and the treachery is real, but it comes from the context and not from this word.

verse.text: And he said, “This is why I have told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to them by the Father.”
Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean either “from this time on” or “as a result of this”. Translations are divided between the two. Both fit the context, and the difference is slight, since the departure follows directly on what Jesus has just said.

verse.text: So Jesus said to the Twelve, “Surely you do not want to go away as well?”
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have words of eternal life,

text.q: and we have come to believe and to know that you are the Holy One of God.”

note.traditional: that Christ, the Son of the living God

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “the Holy One of God”. Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, have “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, which most scholars regard as a harmonisation with Peter’s confession in Matthew 16:16. Elsewhere in the Gospels this title is used of Jesus only by an unclean spirit (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34).

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil.”
He was speaking of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot; for this man, one of the Twelve, was going to hand him over.
After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He did not want to go about in Judea, because the Judeans were seeking to kill him.
verse.note: The Greek word names a people with a religion and a homeland, and John uses it in more than one way. Here the contrast is geographic, Judea as against Galilee, so 'Judeans' is used. In verses 11, 13 and 15 the group is the Jerusalem authorities, as opposed to the festival crowds, who were themselves Jewish, so 'the Jewish leaders' is used there. Most translations have 'the Jews' throughout, and scholars are divided on the best English.

verse.text: Now the Jews’ Festival of Booths was near.
verse.note: This was the week-long autumn pilgrimage festival (Sukkot), when people lived in temporary shelters to recall the wilderness years and to celebrate the harvest. 'Booths' is used because 'tabernacles' no longer suggests a hut to most readers. Later Jewish sources describe daily water-pouring rites at this festival, which may lie behind Jesus's words about thirst and living water in verses 37–38.

verse.text: So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, so that your disciples too may see the works you are doing.

text.q: For no one does anything in secret while he himself seeks to be in the open. If you are doing these things, show yourself to the world.”

verse.text: For not even his brothers believed in him.
So Jesus said to them, “My time has not yet arrived, but your time is always ready.

text.q: The world cannot hate you, but it hates me, because I testify about it that its works are evil.
You go up to the festival. I am not going up to this festival, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.”

note.traditional: I am not yet going up

verse.note: Many manuscripts, including some of the earliest, read 'not yet' instead of 'not'. Many editors prefer 'not' as the harder reading, which scribes may have softened because Jesus does go up in verse 10; others regard 'not yet' as original. The decision is disputed.

verse.text: Having said this, he stayed behind in Galilee.
But when his brothers had gone up to the festival, then he too went up, not publicly but, as it were, in secret.
So the Jewish leaders were looking for him at the festival and saying, “Where is that man?”
And there was much murmuring about him among the crowds. Some were saying, “He is a good man.” Others were saying, “No, he is leading the crowd astray.”
Yet no one spoke openly about him, for fear of the Jewish leaders.
When the festival was already half over, Jesus went up to the temple and began to teach.
So the Jewish leaders were amazed and said, “How is this man so learned, when he has never studied?”
verse.note: The Greek says literally that he 'knows letters', an idiom for being educated. The surprise is not that Jesus can read but that he teaches Scripture like a trained scholar without having studied under a recognised teacher.

verse.text: So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine but belongs to the one who sent me.

text.q: If anyone is willing to do his will, that person will know about the teaching, whether it is from God or whether I speak on my own.
The one who speaks on his own seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no falsehood in him.
Did not Moses give you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why are you seeking to kill me?”

verse.text: The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?”
Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you are all amazed.

text.q: For this reason Moses has given you circumcision—not that it comes from Moses, but from the fathers—and you circumcise a person on the Sabbath.

verse.note: These words can be attached to the end of verse 21 instead: 'you are all amazed because of it. Moses has given you circumcision…'. Several modern translations take them that way or leave them untranslated. The rendering here follows the punctuation of the Greek edition being translated, on which Jesus points to circumcision on the Sabbath as given with a purpose that his healing fulfils.

text.q: If a person receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses is not broken, are you angry with me because I made a whole person well on the Sabbath?
Do not judge by appearance, but judge with just judgment.”

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). Since the subject here is judging fairly, 'just' is used. Older translations have 'righteous judgment'.

verse.text: So some of the people of Jerusalem were saying, “Is this not the man they are seeking to kill?

text.q: And look, he is speaking openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers have truly come to know that this is the Messiah?

verse.note: The Greek word means the anointed king Israel expected, and in this chapter it is a title under debate, not a name. 'Messiah' conveys that to a modern reader; 'Christ' is kept where the word functions as a name for Jesus. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: But we know where this man is from; when the Messiah comes, no one knows where he is from.”

verse.text: So Jesus cried out as he was teaching in the temple, “You know me, and you know where I am from. Yet I have not come on my own; rather, the one who sent me is true, and you do not know him.

text.q: I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.”

verse.text: So they were seeking to seize him, yet no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.
But many of the crowd believed in him, and they were saying, “When the Messiah comes, surely he will not do more signs than this man has done?”
The Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring these things about him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to seize him.
So Jesus said, “I am with you a little while longer, and then I am going to the one who sent me.

text.q: You will look for me and will not find me, and where I am you cannot come.”

verse.text: So the Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go, that we will not find him? Surely he does not intend to go to the Diaspora among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?
verse.note: The 'Diaspora' was the standard term for Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel, here those in the Greek-speaking world. The speakers wonder, scornfully, whether Jesus will go abroad to those communities and even teach non-Jews. 'Greeks' here means Greek-speaking Gentiles.

text.q: What is this saying of his, ‘You will look for me and will not find me, and where I am you cannot come’?”

verse.text: On the last day, the great day of the festival, Jesus stood and cried out, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink.

text.q: Whoever believes in me, as the scripture has said, ‘Rivers of living water will flow from within him.’”

verse.note: The Greek can be punctuated differently: 'Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink. As the scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within him', in which case the rivers flow from Jesus, not from the believer. Both readings are ancient and both have scholarly support. The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used, which is also the more common reading.

The Greek word means the belly or womb and was also used for a person's inner self; many modern versions have 'heart' or 'from within'. No single Old Testament passage matches the quotation. It probably draws together several texts about water flowing in the wilderness and from the temple, and which ones are meant is disputed.

verse.text: Now he said this about the Spirit, which those who had believed in him were going to receive; for as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

note.term: as yet there was no Spirit
note.traditional: the Spirit was not yet given

verse.note: The Greek says simply 'there was not yet Spirit'. Most translations add 'given', as some later manuscripts do. John has already spoken of the Spirit descending on Jesus, so the meaning is not that the Spirit did not exist but that the Spirit was not yet present with believers in the way that followed Jesus's glorification.

verse.text: So some of the crowd, when they heard these words, were saying, “This truly is the Prophet.”
verse.note: This is not 'a prophet' but a particular expected figure: the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18. In John the crowds treat this figure as distinct from the Messiah (compare 1:20–21).

verse.text: Others were saying, “This is the Messiah.” But some were saying, “Surely the Messiah does not come from Galilee?

text.q: Has not the scripture said that the Messiah comes from the offspring of David, and from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”

verse.text: So a division arose in the crowd because of him.
Some of them wanted to seize him, but no one laid hands on him.
So the officers came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?”
The officers answered, “Never has a person spoken like this!”
So the Pharisees answered them, “Surely you have not been led astray as well?

text.q: Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees?
But this crowd that does not know the law—they are accursed.”

verse.text: Nicodemus, the one who had come to him earlier and who was one of them, said to them,

text.q: “Surely our law does not judge a person without first hearing from him and finding out what he is doing?”

verse.text: They answered him, “Surely you are not from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”
Then Jesus spoke to them again: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in the darkness but will have the light of life.”

note.term: Then Jesus spoke to them again

verse.note: The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is not printed here. It is absent from the earliest surviving manuscripts of John and appears at different places in later ones, and the SBLGNT edition translated here does not include it in the main text. Most scholars regard it as an early tradition about Jesus that was not originally part of this Gospel, so verse 12 continues the temple scene of chapter 7.

The setting is still the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 14, 37). Later rabbinic tradition describes great lamps lit in the temple courts during this festival, and many interpreters think the saying alludes to them. The image of God as his people's light is also common in the Scriptures (for example Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 60:19).

verse.text: So the Pharisees said to him, “You are testifying about yourself; your testimony is not true.”
Jesus answered them, “Even if I do testify about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going. But you do not know where I come from or where I am going.

text.q: You judge by human standards; I judge no one.

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'according to the flesh', which formal versions keep. Here 'flesh' means the merely human vantage point, judging by what can be seen, not the body or sinful desire, and a modern reader is likely to hear one of those other senses. Several modern versions render the phrase in the same way as here.

text.q: Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone; it is I and the Father who sent me.
And in your own law it is written that the testimony of two people is true.

note.term: the testimony of two people is true

verse.note: The reference is to the rule in Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15 that a matter must be established by two or three witnesses. Jesus paraphrases the rule and does not quote it word for word. He then applies it by naming himself and the Father as the two witnesses.

text.q: I am the one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.”

verse.text: So they said to him, “Where is your father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father as well.”
He spoke these words in the treasury while teaching in the temple, and no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.
So he said to them again, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.”
So the Jews said, “Surely he is not going to kill himself, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?”
And he said to them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are from this world; I am not from this world.

text.q: That is why I told you that you will die in your sins; for unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.”

verse.note: The Greek says only 'I am', with nothing following. In ordinary speech the phrase can mean 'I am he' or 'it is I', which is why the hearers ask 'Who are you?'. Used without a complement it also echoes God's self-declaration in the Greek version of Isaiah (for example Isaiah 43:10, 'that you may know and believe that I am he'). The same phrase recurs in verse 28 and, with unmistakable force, in verse 58; some translations render all three simply as 'I am'.

verse.text: So they said to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Why am I speaking to you at all?

note.term: Why am I speaking to you at all?
note.traditional: Just what I have been telling you from the beginning

verse.note: This is one of the most obscure sentences in John, and its meaning is disputed. Most English versions take it as a statement: '(I am) what I have been telling you from the beginning'. The rendering here follows the punctuation of the edition translated, which reads it as a question, and takes the opening phrase in its common adverbial sense 'at all'; this reading is also found among early Greek-speaking interpreters. A third option is an exclamation: 'That I speak to you at all!'

text.q: I have much to say about you and much to judge. But the one who sent me is true, and what I have heard from him is what I speak to the world.”

verse.text: They did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father.
So Jesus said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own, but speak these things just as the Father taught me.
verse.note: In John this verb carries a deliberate double sense: being raised up on the cross and being exalted (see 3:14; 12:32–34). The same verb is used of the exaltation of the Lord's servant in the Greek version of Isaiah 52:13.

text.q: And the one who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him.”

verse.text: As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples,

text.q: and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

verse.text: They answered him, “We are Abraham’s descendants and have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will become free’?”
Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I tell you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

text.q: The slave does not remain in the household forever; the son remains forever.
So if the Son sets you free, you will really be free.
I know that you are Abraham’s descendants. Yet you are seeking to kill me, because my word finds no room in you.
I speak of what I have seen in the Father’s presence; and you, then, do what you have heard from your father.”

note.term: do what you have heard from your father

verse.note: In the text translated here neither 'father' has 'my' or 'your', and the verb can be a statement ('you do') or a command ('do'). The alternative reading is an appeal: 'so you too should do what you have heard from the Father'. The rendering here takes the sentence as the first hint of the contrast between two fathers that becomes explicit in verses 41 and 44, which is how the reply in verse 39 seems to understand it. Many later manuscripts add the pronouns to make this sense explicit.

verse.text: They answered him, “Our father is Abraham.” Jesus said to them, “If you are Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works of Abraham.

text.q: But now you are seeking to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this.

verse.text: You are doing the works of your father.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father: God.”
verse.note: The Greek word covers unlawful sexual relations of any kind; many modern versions paraphrase as 'We are not illegitimate children'. In the prophets the same word is a standard image for Israel's unfaithfulness to God through idolatry (Hosea 1:2; 2:4), which fits the claim that follows, to have God alone as Father. Some interpreters also hear a slur on the circumstances of Jesus's own birth, but that is uncertain.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came out from God and am here. I have not come on my own; he sent me.

text.q: Why do you not understand the way I speak? Because you cannot hear my word.

You are from your father the devil, and you want to carry out your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and the father of lies.

note.term: You are from your father the devil

verse.note: The words are addressed to a particular group of hearers in this scene, whom Jesus accuses of seeking his death (verses 37, 40). The dispute is among Jews: Jesus and his earliest followers were themselves Jewish. The argument turns on likeness of conduct, not ancestry (verse 39), and such sharp language about parentage is found in other Jewish polemic of the period. The verse has a long history of being used against Jewish people as a whole, which the context does not support.

text.q: But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me.
Which of you can convict me of sin? If I am telling the truth, why do you not believe me?
Whoever is from God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you are not from God.”

verse.text: The Jews answered him, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”
Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon. I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.

text.q: I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and who judges.
Truly, truly, I tell you: if anyone keeps my word, they will never see death.”

verse.text: The Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and so did the prophets, yet you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, they will never taste death.’

text.q: Surely you are not greater than our father Abraham, who died? The prophets died too. Who do you make yourself out to be?”

verse.text: Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, the one of whom you say, ‘He is our God.’

text.q: Yet you have not come to know him, but I know him. If I said that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him, and I keep his word.
Your father Abraham was overjoyed that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

verse.text: So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?”
Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

note.term: before Abraham came to be, I am
