verse.note: The Greek contrasts two verbs: Abraham 'came into being' (that is, was born), while Jesus simply 'is'. The traditional 'before Abraham was' blurs that contrast. The unqualified 'I am' echoes God's self-declarations in the Greek version of Isaiah, and many interpreters also hear Exodus 3:14. The attempt at stoning in the next verse shows the hearers took it as a claim no mere human could make.

verse.text: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
As he was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth.
His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered, “Neither this man sinned nor his parents; rather, it was so that the works of God might be displayed in him.

note.traditional: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him

verse.note: The Greek has only ‘but so that’, with no verb; ‘it was’ is supplied, as in most translations, making the blindness serve God’s purpose. Some interpreters instead read the clause as describing an outcome, not a purpose. Others attach it to the next sentence: ‘But so that the works of God may be displayed in him, we must work…’. The ancient manuscripts had no punctuation to settle the matter.

text.q: We must work the works of the one who sent me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work.

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read ‘we must work’, drawing the disciples into Jesus’s task; many later manuscripts read ‘I must work’, which is the form familiar from the King James Version. ‘We’ is generally judged original, since copyists would more readily smooth it to match ‘the one who sent me’ than the reverse.

text.q: As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

verse.text: When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, and smeared the mud on the man’s eyes,
and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). So he went and washed, and came back seeing.
verse.note: Siloam was a pool at the southern end of Jerusalem, fed by a channel from the Gihon spring. John connects its name with the Hebrew verb ‘to send’; in this Gospel Jesus is repeatedly called the one whom the Father sent, as in verse 4, so the gloss is probably meant to be heard as more than a geographical aside.

verse.text: Then the neighbors and those who had seen him before, when he was a beggar, began saying, “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?”
Some said, “It is him.” Others said, “No, but he looks like him.” The man himself kept saying, “I am the one.”
verse.note: The Greek is simply ‘I am’ (egō eimi), the ordinary way of saying ‘It’s me’. They are the same two words Jesus uses in the weightier statement at 8:58, but here they are plain self-identification by the healed man.

verse.text: So they asked him, “How were your eyes opened?”
He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud and smeared it on my eyes and told me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed, and I gained my sight.”
They said to him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.”
They brought the man who had once been blind to the Pharisees.
Now it was a Sabbath on the day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.
verse.note: The narrator mentions the mud deliberately. Kneading is listed among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath in later rabbinic tradition, and treating a condition that was not life-threatening on the Sabbath was also disputed. This explains the charge in verse 16 that Jesus does not keep the Sabbath.

verse.text: So the Pharisees also asked him again how he had gained his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”

So some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a person who is a sinner perform such signs?” And there was a division among them.
So they said to the blind man again, “What do you say about him, since it was your eyes he opened?” He said, “He is a prophet.”
The Jewish leaders, then, did not believe that he had been blind and had gained his sight, until they summoned the parents of the man who had gained his sight
verse.note: The Greek word is ‘the Jews’, but everyone in this story is Jewish: the man, his parents, the neighbors and Jesus. The group meant here is the authorities who conduct the inquiry and can impose penalties (verse 22), apparently the same people called Pharisees in verses 13–16. Scholars are divided on how best to render the term in John; some prefer ‘Judeans’, others keep ‘the Jews’ throughout.

verse.text: and asked them, “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”
His parents answered, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind;

text.q: but how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”

verse.text: His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders, for the Jewish leaders had already agreed that anyone who acknowledged him as Messiah would be put out of the synagogue.
verse.note: The Greek christos is here a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and not a name; the question is whether Jesus is that figure. ‘Messiah’ conveys the title to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

The Greek is a single adjective, found only in John (here, 12:42 and 16:2), meaning ‘excluded from the synagogue’, that is, cut off from the local Jewish community and its common life. Many scholars think the verse reflects conflicts between synagogues and Jesus’s followers in the decades after his death; others hold that local, informal exclusion was possible in his lifetime. The question is disputed.

verse.text: That is why his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”
So for a second time they summoned the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.”
verse.note: This is not an invitation to thank God for the healing. It is a solemn formula charging a person to tell the truth or own up, as when Joshua says the same to Achan in Joshua 7:19. The interrogators are demanding that the man admit Jesus is a sinner.

verse.text: He answered, “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I know: I was blind, and now I see.”
So they said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”
He answered them, “I told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Surely you don’t want to become his disciples too?”
They hurled abuse at him and said, “You are that man’s disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.

text.q: We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.”

verse.text: The man answered them, “Why, this is the astonishing thing: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes.

text.q: We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is devout and does his will, God listens to that person.
Never since time began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a person born blind.
If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

verse.text: They answered him, “You were born wholly in sins, and you are teaching us?” And they threw him out.
Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and when he found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read ‘Son of Man’; most later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘Son of God’. ‘Son of Man’ is almost certainly original, since copyists would naturally replace it with the more usual object of belief and are unlikely to have done the opposite.

verse.text: He answered, “And who is he, sir, so that I may believe in him?”
verse.note: The same Greek address, kyrie, appears in verses 36 and 38. It ranges from a polite ‘sir’ to ‘Lord’ as a confession. In verse 36 the man does not yet know who the Son of Man is, so ‘sir’ fits; in verse 38, after Jesus identifies himself and the man declares his belief, ‘Lord’ is used. The shift is an interpretive choice that English forces and the Greek does not mark.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “You have seen him; in fact, he is the one speaking with you.”
He said, “I believe, Lord,” and he bowed down before him.
verse.note: The Greek verb denotes the physical act of prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king or another person of high rank; the English ‘worship’ has narrowed to religious devotion alone. Most translations have ‘worshiped’, and many interpreters think John intends that full sense here, following the man’s confession. A few early manuscripts lack verse 38 and the opening words of verse 39, though most scholars regard them as original.

verse.text: And Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.”
Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him, “Surely we are not blind too?”
Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin. But now you say, ‘We see.’ Your sin remains.”

text.q: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate but climbs in some other way is a thief and a bandit.

verse.note: The Greek word covers any doorway or entrance. The older English tradition has “door”, which gives “I am the door” in verses 7 and 9. Because the entrance here is to a walled enclosure for sheep, “gate” is the natural English word, and several modern translations use it.

The traditional rendering is “robber”. In the period the word regularly means an armed brigand who takes by violence, as distinct from the thief who takes by stealth. The pairing therefore covers both stealth and force.

text.q: But the one who enters through the gate is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
When he has brought out all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.
A stranger they will never follow; they will run away from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.”

verse.text: Jesus told them this figure of speech, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verse.note: Older versions have “parable”, but this is not the word the other Gospels use for Jesus’s parables. It means a proverb or a veiled, figurative saying, and John contrasts it with plain speech in 16:25 and 16:29. Many modern translations also have “figure of speech”.

verse.text: So Jesus spoke to them again: “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep.

text.q: All who came before me are thieves and bandits, but the sheep did not listen to them.
I am the gate. Whoever enters through me will be saved, and will come in and go out and find pasture.
The thief comes only to steal and slaughter and destroy. I came so that they may have life, and have it in abundance.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
The hired hand, who is not a shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and runs away—and the wolf snatches them and scatters them—
because he is a hired hand and does not care about the sheep.
I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me,
just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.
I have other sheep too, which are not of this fold. I must bring them as well, and they will listen to my voice, and they will become one flock, with one shepherd.

verse.note: The King James Version has “one fold”, following the Latin, but the Greek word here means “flock” and is a different word from “fold” earlier in the verse. The Greek plays on flock (poimnē) and shepherd (poimēn). The picture is of sheep from more than one fold becoming one flock, not of a single enclosure.

text.q: This is why the Father loves me: because I lay down my life, so that I may take it up again.
No one takes it from me; I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This command I received from my Father.”

verse.text: Again a division arose among the Jews because of these words.
Many of them were saying, “He has a demon and is out of his mind. Why listen to him?”
Others were saying, “These are not the words of someone possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”
Then came the Festival of Dedication in Jerusalem. It was winter,
verse.note: This is Hanukkah, the eight-day winter festival commemorating the rededication of the Jerusalem temple in 164 BC after its desecration under Antiochus IV. The setting gives point to Jesus’s description of himself in verse 36 as the one the Father “consecrated”.

verse.text: and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s Colonnade.
So the Jews surrounded him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.”
verse.note: Literally, “How long are you taking away our life?” Most translators understand the idiom as “keep us in suspense”. Some take it as “How long will you provoke us?”, which suits a hostile crowd. The phrase echoes verse 18, where no one “takes” Jesus’s life from him.

The traditional rendering is “the Christ”. Here the word is a title under discussion, the anointed king Israel expected, and “Messiah” conveys what a first-century Jewish hearer would have understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it works as a name.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me;

text.q: but you do not believe, because you are not among my sheep.
My sheep listen to my voice, and I know them, and they follow me,
and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age”, and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come. It describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here.

text.q: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand.

note.term: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all
note.traditional: My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all

verse.note: The manuscripts differ here in both the relative pronoun and the form of “greater”, and the Greek as printed is hard to construe. The other main reading is “What my Father has given me is greater than all”, which some modern translations adopt or give in a footnote. The rendering here follows the sense most translations adopt, which suits the next clause about the Father’s hand.

text.q: I and the Father are one.”

verse.note: “One” is neuter in Greek, “one thing”, not masculine, “one person”. In context the immediate point is that Jesus and the Father act as one in keeping the sheep. The hearers’ reaction in verses 31–33 shows they heard a larger claim, and later theology drew on the verse for the unity of Father and Son.

verse.text: Again the Jews picked up stones to stone him.
Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?”
The Jews answered him, “We are not stoning you for a good work but for blasphemy, because you, a human being, make yourself God.”
verse.note: The Greek noun has no article and could be read “make yourself a god”. Jesus’s reply from the psalm (“you are gods”) plays on that wider sense. Most translations render “God”, since the charge is blasphemy against Israel’s one God.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your law, ‘I said, you are gods’?
verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 82:6, so “law” is used here in the broad sense of Scripture as a whole. In the psalm God addresses beings called “gods”. They have been understood as Israel’s judges, as Israel at Sinai, or as members of a heavenly council. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture can use the word of them, the one the Father sent does not blaspheme by saying “I am God’s Son”.

text.q: If he called them gods, those to whom the word of God came—and the Scripture cannot be set aside—
do you say to the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am God’s Son’?
If I am not doing my Father’s works, do not believe me.
But if I am doing them, then even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may come to know and keep on knowing that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

note.term: come to know and keep on knowing

verse.note: The Greek uses the same verb twice in two tenses, the first for arriving at knowledge and the second for continuing in it. Most translations vary the English (“know and understand”). The rendering here keeps the repetition and the difference of aspect.

verse.text: So they tried again to seize him, but he escaped out of their hands.
He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and he stayed there.
Many came to him and were saying, “John performed no sign, but everything John said about this man was true.”
And many believed in him there.
Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.
Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with perfumed oil and wiped his feet with her hair; it was her brother Lazarus who was ill.
So the sisters sent word to him, saying, “Lord, look, the one you love is ill.”
verse.note: Two Greek verbs for love appear in this chapter: one here and in verse 36, another in verse 5. Some interpreters see a distinction between warm affection and a higher love. Most scholars judge that John uses the two interchangeably, and both are rendered 'love' here.

verse.text: When Jesus heard this, he said, “This illness is not to end in death; it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”
Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.
So when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed for the time being in the place where he was, two days.
Then, after this, he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”
The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, just now the Judeans were trying to stone you, and you are going back there?”
verse.note: The Greek word covers both 'Jews' and 'Judeans'. Here the contrast is geographic: Jesus is across the Jordan and proposes returning to Judea, where people had tried to stone him. Elsewhere in the chapter the same word is rendered 'Jews'. Scholars are divided: some argue for 'Judeans' throughout, others object that this erases Jews from the New Testament.

verse.text: Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, they do not stumble, because they see the light of this world.

text.q: But if anyone walks in the night, they stumble, because the light is not in them.”

verse.text: He said this, and after that he told them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going to wake him.”
So the disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will get well.”
verse.note: The verb is the one usually translated 'save'; used of a sick person it ordinarily means 'recover'. The disciples mean only that sleep is a good sign. A reader of the Greek may well have heard the larger sense too, in keeping with the misunderstandings John often builds into dialogue.

verse.text: Now Jesus had been speaking about his death, but they thought he was speaking about ordinary sleep.
So then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,

text.q: and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”

verse.text: So Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.”
verse.note: Didymus is the ordinary Greek word for 'twin', and the name Thomas reflects the Aramaic word with the same meaning. John is explaining the name for Greek readers, so it is translated here. Many English versions leave it as 'Didymus'.

verse.text: When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.
verse.note: Burial normally took place on the day of death. Later rabbinic tradition records a belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days. If that idea was already current, which is uncertain, the fourth day marks the death as beyond all doubt; Martha's remark in verse 39 makes the same point in physical terms.

verse.text: Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles away,
verse.note: The Greek says 'about fifteen stadia'. A stadion was roughly 185 metres, so the distance is a little under three kilometres, or somewhat less than two miles.

verse.text: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother.
So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him, but Mary remained seated in the house.
Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.

text.q: And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise.”
Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.”
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if they die, will live,

text.q: and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

verse.text: She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world.”
verse.note: The Greek word is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, and Martha is confessing that Jesus holds that title. 'Messiah' conveys this to a modern reader, for whom 'Christ' sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep 'Christ' where it works as a name.

verse.text: When she had said this, she went away and called her sister Mary, telling her privately, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”
When Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to him.
Now Jesus had not yet come into the village but was still at the place where Martha had met him.
So the Jews who were with her in the house consoling her, when they saw Mary get up quickly and go out, followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.
When Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he was stirred to anger in spirit and troubled,

note.traditional: groaned in the spirit / was deeply moved in spirit

verse.note: Elsewhere in the New Testament this verb is used of stern warning or angry rebuke (Mark 1:43; 14:5), and in wider Greek of snorting with anger. Most English versions soften it to 'deeply moved', but many commentators hold that indignation is meant. The text does not say what the anger is directed at: death itself, the grief it causes, or the unbelief of those present have all been proposed. The verb recurs in verse 38.

verse.text: and he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”
Jesus burst into tears.
verse.note: The verb differs from the one used of Mary and the mourners in verses 31 and 33, which is the usual word for audible lamentation. This one means to shed tears and occurs only here in the New Testament; its tense suggests the onset of the action. 'Jesus wept' is the familiar rendering, but it hides the change of verb.

verse.text: So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”
But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man have done something so that this man also would not die?”
Then Jesus, again stirred to anger within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by now there is a stench, for it is the fourth day.”
Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believe you will see the glory of God?”
So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted his eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.

text.q: I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

verse.text: When he had said this, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”
The dead man came out, his feet and hands bound with burial wrappings and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Untie him and let him go.”
So many of the Jews, those who had come to Mary and seen what he did, believed in him.
But some of them went off to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
So the chief priests and the Pharisees called a meeting of the council and said, “What are we doing? This man is performing many signs.

text.q: If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

verse.note: 'Place' most likely means the temple, which Jewish writing of the period often calls 'the place' or 'the holy place'. It could also mean Jerusalem, or the council's own standing. The rendering leaves the Greek as open as it is.

This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually rendered 'Gentiles'; here, in the singular, it means the Jewish nation as a political body. In verse 50 Caiaphas sets it beside a different word, rendered 'the people', which often refers to Israel as God's people.

verse.text: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all,
verse.note: The high priesthood was not an annual office, and Caiaphas held it for about eighteen years (roughly AD 18 to 36). Most scholars take John to mean 'in that fateful year', the year of Jesus's death, not that the office changed hands yearly.

text.q: nor do you consider that it is to your advantage that one man should die for the people and the whole nation not perish.”

verse.text: He did not say this on his own, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation,
and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.
So from that day on they planned to kill him.
So Jesus no longer walked about openly among the Jews, but went away from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and he stayed there with the disciples.
Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up to Jerusalem from the countryside before the Passover to purify themselves.
So they were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival?”
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it, so that they could arrest him.
Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.
So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha was serving, and Lazarus was one of those reclining at the table with him.
Then Mary took a pound of very costly perfumed oil, pure nard, and anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped his feet with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfumed oil.
verse.note: The Greek adjective is rare and its meaning is uncertain. Most scholars take it as “genuine” or “unadulterated”, which suits an expensive import that was often diluted; other proposals are “liquid” or a trade name for a kind of nard. Mark 14:3 uses the same phrase. The “pound” is the Roman pound, about 325 grams or twelve ounces.

verse.text: But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, the one who was about to hand him over, said,
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for handing a person or thing over to someone else, and the Gospels use it of Jesus being handed over by Judas, by the chief priests and by Pilate alike. English tradition renders it “betray” when Judas is the subject, a fair inference from the story but narrower than the word itself. The standard lexicons give “hand over, deliver up” as its meaning.

text.q: “Why wasn’t this perfumed oil sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”

note.traditional: three hundred pence; a year’s wages

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a laborer. Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year’s wages for a working man.

verse.text: He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief; he kept the money box and used to take what was put into it.

note.traditional: bare what was put therein; used to help himself to what was put into it

verse.note: The verb means “carry” and can also mean “carry off”, that is, steal. The sentence could say only that Judas carried the common fund, but coming straight after “he was a thief” most scholars read it as pilfering, and the translation follows them.

verse.text: So Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.

note.term: so that she may keep it for the day of my burial
note.traditional: against the day of my burying hath she kept this

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and its sense is disputed. It may mean “let her keep it for the day of my burial”, or, with words supplied, “she did not sell it so that she could keep it for this”, with the anointing itself anticipating his burial. Later manuscripts smooth the difficulty to “she has kept it”. The word for burial refers to preparing a body for the tomb.

text.q: For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.”

verse.text: A large crowd of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came, not only because of Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.
But the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well,
because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
The next day the large crowd that had come to the festival heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.
They took palm branches and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!”
verse.note: A Hebrew cry meaning “save, please”, from Psalm 118:25, the psalm the crowd goes on to quote. By the first century it was used as a shout of acclamation at festivals, so it is kept as the cry it was and not translated. Palm branches were associated with national celebration and victory.

verse.text: Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, as it is written:

text.q: “Do not be afraid, daughter Zion. Look, your king is coming, seated on a donkey’s colt.”

verse.note: The phrase is a biblical personification of Jerusalem itself as a young woman: Zion is the daughter, not her parent. “Daughter of Zion” is the familiar wording, but it suggests someone who belongs to Zion; several modern translations now use “daughter Zion”. The quotation is a shortened form of Zechariah 9:9.

verse.text: His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and that they had done these things to him.
So the crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead kept bearing witness.

note.term: when he called Lazarus out of the tomb

verse.note: Some early manuscripts read “that” where others read “when”, a difference of one letter in Greek. With “that”, the verse says the crowd with him kept testifying that he had called Lazarus out of the tomb. The edition translated here reads “when”, which makes this crowd the eyewitnesses from Bethany, distinct from the festival crowd of verse 18.

verse.text: This was also why the crowd went to meet him: they had heard that he had done this sign.
So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are getting nowhere. Look, the world has gone after him!”
Now among those who went up to worship at the festival were some Greeks.
They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.”
Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.
Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Whoever loves their life loses it, and whoever hates their life in this world will keep it for eternal life.

verse.note: The word here is the one for a person’s own life or self, the same word rendered “soul” in verse 27. It is a different Greek word from the “life” in “eternal life” at the end of the verse. “Hates” is a Semitic way of expressing sharp preference, putting one thing decisively second to another, and not a call to self-loathing.

In Jewish usage this phrase meant the life of the age to come, the new era God would bring in. It describes a kind of life as well as an unending length of it. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come”.

text.q: If anyone serves me, they must follow me, and where I am, there my servant will be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor them.
Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this hour’? But it was for this that I came to this hour.

note.term: Father, save me from this hour

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, so this can be read either as a prayer Jesus considers and sets aside (“Shall I say, ‘Father, save me’?”) or as a prayer he actually prays and then at once overrides. The edition translated here punctuates it as a statement; most English translations take it as a question, as this one does. On either reading the next sentence gives his decision.

verse.text: Father, glorify your name.” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
The crowd standing there heard it and said it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”
Jesus answered, “This voice has come not for my sake but for yours.

text.q: Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be thrown out.
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”

verse.note: The verb means both to raise something physically and to exalt or honor someone. John uses it with both senses at once: Jesus is raised up on the cross, as verse 33 explains, and that same event is his exaltation. The Greek conjunction is literally “if”, but it expresses no doubt about the event. Some manuscripts read “all things” in place of “all people”.

verse.text: He said this to indicate the kind of death he was going to die.
So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Messiah remains forever. So how can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one” and here is a title for the king Israel expected, not a name for Jesus, so “Messiah” is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels. “The Law” here stands for the Scriptures generally; the crowd is probably thinking of promises that David’s line and kingdom would last forever.

verse.text: So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, so that darkness does not overtake you; whoever walks in the darkness does not know where they are going.
While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become children of light.” Jesus said these things, then went away and hid from them.
Though he had done so many signs in front of them, they did not believe in him,
so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”
For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again:

text.q: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they would not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.”

verse.text: Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke about him.
verse.note: The quotation in verse 40 comes from Isaiah 6, where the prophet sees the Lord enthroned in the temple. “His” and “him” here most naturally refer to Jesus: John is saying that the glory Isaiah saw was Christ’s. Some manuscripts read “when he saw” in place of “because he saw”.

verse.text: Nevertheless, many even among the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not acknowledge it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue;
for they loved the glory that comes from people more than the glory that comes from God.
Then Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in the one who sent me,

text.q: and whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.
I have come into the world as light, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in the darkness.
If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge that person, for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.
Whoever rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge: the word that I have spoken will judge that person on the last day.
For I have not spoken on my own; the Father who sent me has himself given me a command, what to say and what to speak.
And I know that his command is eternal life. So the things I speak, I speak just as the Father has told me.”

verse.text: Now before the Passover festival, Jesus knew that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father; having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean 'to the end' in time (to the last moment of his life) or 'to the utmost, completely'. Both senses are well attested, and many scholars think John intends both. 'To the end' is kept because it leaves room for either reading.

verse.text: And during supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to hand him over,
verse.note: The verb means 'hand over' or 'deliver up'; it is the ordinary word for delivering someone into custody, and Greek has a separate verb for 'betray'. English tradition renders it 'betray' whenever Judas is the subject, which is a fair inference from the story but narrower than the word itself. The same verb is used elsewhere of the authorities handing Jesus over to Pilate.

note.term: put it into the heart of Judas
note.traditional: put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him

verse.note: In the best-attested Greek text the wording is literally 'the devil having already put into the heart that Judas should hand him over', without saying whose heart. Most translators take it as Judas's heart; some scholars take it as the devil's own, meaning the devil had already resolved on it. Later manuscripts reword the phrase so that it is unambiguously Judas's heart.

verse.text: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God,
got up from supper, laid aside his outer garments, and, taking a linen towel, tied it around his waist.
verse.note: The verb for 'laid aside' is the one this Gospel uses for Jesus laying down his life (10:11–18) and for Peter's offer in verses 37–38. The verb for putting the garments back on in verse 12 is the one used there for taking his life up again. Many commentators think the echo is deliberate and that the footwashing acts out his death in advance.

verse.text: Then he poured water into the basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to dry them with the towel that was tied around him.
So he came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, are you going to wash my feet?”
Jesus answered him, “You do not know now what I am doing, but afterward you will understand.”
Peter said to him, “You will never, ever wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “Unless I wash you, you have no share with me.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus said to him, “One who has bathed has no need to wash, except for the feet, but is clean all over. And you are clean, but not all of you.”
verse.note: A few early witnesses, including Codex Sinaiticus, lack these words and read simply 'has no need to wash'. Most manuscripts include them, and most editors and translations keep them, though some scholars regard the shorter text as original.

verse.text: For he knew who was handing him over; that is why he said, “Not all of you are clean.”
So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garments back on, and reclined again, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done for you?

text.q: You call me ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord,’ and you are right to say so, for that is what I am.
So if I, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, so that you also should do just as I have done for you.
Truly, truly I tell you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired servant, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. 'Servant' is the traditional English rendering, and some modern versions keep it. The word for 'master' here is the same one translated 'Lord' in verses 13–14, so the saying applies directly to Jesus and his disciples.

The Greek word is the one elsewhere rendered 'apostle'. This is its only occurrence in John's Gospel, and here it carries its ordinary sense of someone sent on another's behalf, not the title of an office.

text.q: If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
I am not speaking about all of you; I know the ones I have chosen. But this is so that the scripture may be fulfilled: ‘The one who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me.’

note.term: has lifted up his heel against me
note.traditional: hath lifted up his heel against me

verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 41:9, where the speaker is betrayed by a close friend who shared his table. Eating someone's bread implied a bond of loyalty, so the image is of treachery from within the circle of trust. The exact force of 'lifting the heel' is uncertain; it is usually taken as a gesture of contempt or a hostile kick.

text.q: I am telling you now, before it happens, so that when it does happen you may believe that I am he.

verse.note: The Greek is simply 'I am', with no complement. It can mean 'I am the one I claim to be', but it also echoes God's self-declaration in the Greek version of Isaiah (for example 43:10, 'that you may know and believe that I am'). Many scholars hold that John intends the divine echo here; some translations therefore print 'I am'.

text.q: Truly, truly I tell you, whoever receives anyone I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”

verse.text: When he had said this, Jesus was troubled in spirit and testified, “Truly, truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over.”
The disciples looked at one another, at a loss as to whom he meant.
One of his disciples, the one Jesus loved, was reclining at Jesus’s side.
verse.note: At formal meals diners reclined on their left side on low couches, so the person on one's right lay with his head near one's chest; this is how the disciple can lean back and speak privately in verse 25. The Greek says literally 'in Jesus's bosom', the same expression used in 1:18 of the Son's place with the Father.

verse.text: So Simon Peter nodded to him to ask who it was that he was speaking about.
That disciple, leaning back just as he was against Jesus’s chest, said to him, “Lord, who is it?”
Jesus answered, “It is the one for whom I will dip the piece of bread and give it to him.” So, having dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot.
And after the piece of bread, Satan then entered into him. So Jesus said to him, “What you are doing, do quickly.”
But none of those reclining at the table knew why he said this to him.
Some supposed, since Judas kept the money box, that Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the festival,” or that he should give something to the poor.
So, having taken the piece of bread, he went out at once. And it was night.
When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.

text.q: If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him at once.

note.term: If God has been glorified in him
note.traditional: If God be glorified in him

verse.note: This opening clause is absent from several of the earliest and best manuscripts. It may have been dropped accidentally because it repeats the end of the previous verse, or added later to smooth the logic. The edition translated here includes it, and scholars remain divided.

text.q: Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. You will look for me, and just as I told the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say it to you as well.
A new commandment I give you: that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

verse.text: Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow later.”
Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”
Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly I tell you, a rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.”

text.q: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me.

note.term: Believe in God; believe also in me.
note.traditional: ye believe in God, believe also in me

verse.note: The Greek verb form used twice here can be either a statement ('you believe') or a command ('believe'). Both are taken as commands here, which suits the opening 'Do not let your hearts be troubled'. The older tradition took the first as a statement and the second as a command, and that remains possible. The verb also carries the sense 'trust'.

text.q: In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places. If there were not, I would have told you; for I am going to prepare a place for you.

verse.note: The word means a place where one stays or lives. In this Gospel it echoes the verb 'remain' that runs through these chapters. 'Mansions' once meant simply 'lodgings' but now suggests grand houses, which the Greek does not. The same word returns in verse 23, where the Father and the Son 'make our dwelling' with the one who loves Jesus.

note.term: I would have told you; for I am going
note.traditional: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you

verse.note: The Greek can be punctuated in more than one way. It may also be read as a question: 'If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going to prepare a place for you?' Several modern translations take it that way. The rendering here follows the punctuation of the Greek edition translated, taking the connecting word as 'for' rather than 'that'.

text.q: And if I go and prepare a place for you, I am coming again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.
And where I am going, you know the way.”

verse.text: Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
Jesus said to him, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

text.q: If you had known me, you would have known my Father as well. From now on you do know him, and you have seen him.”

note.term: If you had known me, you would have known my Father as well.
note.traditional: If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also

verse.note: Manuscripts differ here. Some early witnesses read 'If you have come to know me, you will know my Father also', which makes the sentence a promise rather than a mild reproach. The edition translated here adopts the reproach, which fits the question put to Philip in verse 9. Editors remain divided.

verse.text: Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”
Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you have not come to know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?

text.q: Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own; but the Father, remaining in me, does his works.
Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me; or if not, believe because of the works themselves.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.
And whatever you ask in my name, I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
If you ask me for anything in my name, I will do it.

note.term: If you ask me for anything
note.traditional: If ye shall ask any thing in my name

verse.note: Many manuscripts lack the word 'me', and a few omit the whole verse. The reading with 'me' has strong early support. It may have been dropped because asking Jesus 'in my name' seemed awkward, or to match 16:23.

text.q: If you love me, you will keep my commandments.

verse.note: Many manuscripts have a command here ('keep my commandments'), and the King James tradition follows them. The edition translated here reads a future, 'you will keep', which makes obedience the outcome of love rather than a demand. The two forms differ by only a letter or two in Greek.

text.q: And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you forever:

verse.note: In Greek usage of the period the word describes someone called in to speak or act on another's behalf, and 1 John 2:1 uses it of Jesus in exactly that sense. 'Comforter' comes from older English, where it meant 'strengthener', and now suggests consolation only. Current translations are divided between 'Advocate', 'Helper' and 'Counselor'. 'Another' implies that Jesus himself has been the first.

text.q: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, because he remains with you and will be in you.
I will not leave you orphans; I am coming to you.
A little while longer and the world will see me no more, but you will see me; because I live, you also will live.
On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.
Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, that is the one who loves me. And the one who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I too will love that person and reveal myself to them.”

verse.text: Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, what has happened, that you are going to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?”
verse.note: Judas was a very common name. This is a second disciple of that name, probably the 'Judas of James' in Luke's lists of the Twelve (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), and often identified with Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark. Judas Iscariot has already left the meal (13:30).

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, they will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our dwelling with them.

text.q: Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.
I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.
But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you.
Peace I leave with you; my own peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them be afraid.
You heard me say to you, ‘I am going away, and I am coming to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I am.
And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe.
I will no longer speak much with you, for the ruler of the world is coming. He has no claim on me,

note.term: He has no claim on me

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'in me he has nothing'. This is generally understood as an idiom, probably reflecting a Semitic legal expression, for having no claim against or hold over someone. Modern versions vary between 'no claim on me', 'no power over me' and 'no hold over me'. The literal wording is now obscure in English.

text.q: but so that the world may know that I love the Father, I do just as the Father has commanded me. Get up; let us go from here.”

note.term: but so that the world may know that I love the Father, I do just as the Father has commanded me
note.traditional: But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do

verse.note: The Greek sentence is compressed and can be construed in more than one way. Alternatively, a main clause is to be supplied: '(this is happening) so that the world may know that I love the Father and that I do just as the Father commanded me.' On either reading the point is that Jesus goes to his death out of obedience, not because the ruler of the world has power over him.

note.term: Get up; let us go from here.

verse.note: Jesus appears to end the meal here, yet the discourse continues for three more chapters, and the group crosses the Kidron valley only at 18:1. Some scholars think chapters 15 to 17 were spoken on the way. Others think they were spoken while the group lingered. Many hold that the Gospel combines more than one version of the farewell discourse. The question is unresolved.

text.q: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.

verse.note: In Israel’s Scriptures the vine or vineyard is a standing image for Israel itself, planted and tended by God and often rebuked for failing to bear good fruit (for example Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5). A first-century Jewish reader would hear Jesus’ claim to be the “true” vine against that background.

text.q: Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes clean so that it may bear more fruit.

verse.note: The verb can mean either “take away, remove” or “lift up.” Some interpreters argue that the vinegrower lifts fruitless branches off the ground so that they can bear. Most scholars take it as removal, which fits verse 6, and that reading is followed here.

The Greek verb means “to cleanse” and is here applied to clearing a vine. It is the verb behind the adjective “clean” in the next verse, and it also chimes in sound with “takes away” (airei / kathairei). “Prunes clean” keeps the link to verse 3 visible, which the plain “prunes” of most versions hides.

text.q: You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you.
Remain in me, and I in you. Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.

verse.note: The traditional “abide” is now archaic and has a devotional colouring the Greek word lacks. It is the ordinary verb for staying or remaining somewhere, and it occurs eleven times in this chapter. “Remain” is used throughout, including for the fruit that “remains” in verse 16, so that the repetition can be heard.

text.q: I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in them, bears much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
Whoever does not remain in me is thrown out like a branch and withers; such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire and burned.
If you remain in me and my words remain in you, ask for whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.
In this my Father is glorified: that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.

note.traditional: so shall ye be my disciples

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between a subjunctive (“that you … become my disciples”) and a future (“and you will become my disciples”). The edition translated here reads the subjunctive. The sense is that bearing fruit is how they come to be, or show themselves to be, his disciples.

text.q: “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you. Remain in my love.
If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.
I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be made full.
“This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.
No one has greater love than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
You are my friends if you do what I command you.
I no longer call you slaves, because a slave does not know what his master is doing. I have called you friends, because everything I heard from my Father I have made known to you.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, someone owned by a master, not a hired servant. The contrast with “friends” depends on this: a slave is given orders without explanations, while a friend is taken into confidence. Many recent versions still have “servants,” though “slaves” is widely acknowledged to be the more accurate sense.

text.q: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that remains, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name he may give you.
These things I command you so that you will love one another.
“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.

verse.note: The Greek form can be either a command (“know that”) or a statement (“you know that”). Most modern versions and commentators take it as a command, as here; the King James Version read it as a statement.

text.q: If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, for that reason the world hates you.
Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘A slave is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too; if they kept my word, they will keep yours too.
But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me.
If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.
Whoever hates me hates my Father also.
If I had not done among them the works that no one else has done, they would have no sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.
But this is so that the word written in their law may be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause.’

verse.note: “Law” is used here in the broad sense of the Jewish Scriptures as a whole, since the words quoted come from the Psalms (see Psalms 35:19 and 69:4), not the five books of Moses. “Their law” means the Scriptures that the opponents themselves acknowledge.

text.q: “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who comes forth from the Father, he will testify about me.

verse.note: Outside the New Testament the word is used of someone called in to speak on another’s behalf, and 1 John 2:1 clearly uses it that way of Jesus. That sense suits this verse, where the Advocate gives testimony. “Advocate,” “Helper” and “Counselor” are all in current use among translations; “Comforter” goes back to the older English versions.

text.q: And you also testify, because you have been with me from the beginning.

verse.note: The Greek form can be a statement (“you are testifying”) or a command (“you too must testify”), and translations differ. The present tense is kept here, and the English, like the Greek, can be read either way.

text.q: “I have said these things to you so that you will not fall away.
They will put you out of the synagogue. Indeed, an hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think they are offering worship to God.

note.term: put you out of the synagogue

verse.note: The Greek is a single adjective meaning 'expelled from the synagogue', found in the New Testament only in John (also 9:22 and 12:42). The synagogue was the centre of Jewish communal life, so exclusion meant loss of standing in the community and not merely of a place to worship.

text.q: And they will do these things because they have not come to know the Father or me.
But I have said these things to you so that when their hour comes you will remember that I told you about them. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.
“But now I am going to the one who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’
Instead, because I have said these things to you, pain has filled your heart.

verse.note: One Greek word, covering both grief of mind and bodily pain, runs through verses 6, 20, 21 and 22, and the argument turns on the link between the disciples' state and a woman's labour. 'Pain' is used throughout so that the repetition is visible. Most versions have 'sorrow' or 'grief' for the disciples, and some switch to 'pain' for the woman.

text.q: But I am telling you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.

verse.note: The traditional 'Comforter' goes back to the early English versions. In Greek of the period the word describes someone called in to speak or act on another's behalf, and 1 John 2:1 uses it of Jesus in that sense; the courtroom colouring suits verses 8–11 here. 'Helper' and 'Counselor' are also in current use.

text.q: And when he comes, he will show the world to be in the wrong about sin and about righteousness and about judgment:

note.term: show the world to be in the wrong

verse.note: The verb means to expose, to bring a fault to light, or to prove someone wrong, often in a legal setting. Many versions have 'convict the world concerning', which fits sin but sits awkwardly with righteousness and judgment; the rendering here lets one verb govern all three. The Greek does not settle whether the world is itself persuaded or is simply shown up as wrong.

text.q: about sin, because they do not believe in me;
about righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me;

verse.note: Whose righteousness is meant is not stated. Most interpreters take it as Jesus' own: his going to the Father shows that he, whom the world condemned, was in the right. Others take it as the world's mistaken idea of what righteousness is.

text.q: and about judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged.
“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
But when he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you in all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but will speak whatever he hears, and he will declare to you the things that are coming.

verse.note: Manuscripts divide between 'in all the truth' and 'into all the truth'. The Greek text translated here reads 'in', which pictures guidance within the whole sphere of truth rather than arrival at it. The difference in meaning is slight.

text.q: He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and declare it to you.
Everything the Father has is mine; that is why I said that he takes from what is mine and will declare it to you.
“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.”

verse.text: So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he is saying to us, ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ‘Because I am going to the Father’?”
So they kept saying, “What is this ‘little while’ he speaks of? We do not know what he is talking about.”

Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, and he said to them, “Is this what you are discussing with one another, that I said, ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’?

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be in pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
When a woman is giving birth she has pain, because her hour has come; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the distress, for joy that a human being has been born into the world.
So you too have pain now; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you.
And on that day you will ask me nothing. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father for, he will give it to you in my name.

verse.note: The verb can mean either 'ask a question' or 'ask for something'. Since the disciples have just been unsure how to question him (verses 17–19), many take it as 'you will ask me no more questions'; others take it as 'you will make no request of me', in contrast with asking the Father. A different Greek verb, used of requests, follows in the second half of the verse.

note.term: he will give it to you in my name
note.traditional: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you

verse.note: Manuscripts differ on where 'in my name' stands. In the Greek text translated here it follows 'he will give it to you'. In many other manuscripts it is attached to 'ask', as in verse 24 and as most English versions have it.

text.q: Until now you have asked for nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be full.
“I have said these things to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech, but will tell you plainly about the Father.

verse.note: This is the Septuagint's word for a proverb and gave the book of Proverbs its Greek title; older English versions have 'proverbs' here. John uses it for veiled or figurative speech that needs explaining, in contrast with speaking plainly.

text.q: On that day you will ask in my name, and I am not saying to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;
for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.
I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”

verse.text: His disciples said, “Look, now you are speaking plainly and using no figure of speech!

text.q: Now we know that you know everything and have no need for anyone to ask you questions. By this we believe that you came from God.”

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?
verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, so this can be read either as a question or as a statement: 'Now you believe.' Either way, the next verse shows that Jesus regards the disciples' confidence as premature.

text.q: Look, an hour is coming, and has come, when you will be scattered, each to your own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.
I have said these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have distress; but take courage: I have conquered the world.”

verse.text: After Jesus had said these things, he lifted his eyes to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come. Glorify your Son, so that the Son may glorify you,

text.q: just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him.

verse.note: A Semitic expression, familiar from the Greek Old Testament, for all humanity, often with a hint of human frailty before God. Many modern translations paraphrase it as 'all people'. The literal phrase is kept here because the Greek keeps it.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age', and in Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come: a kind of life as well as an unending one. Verse 3 gives this Gospel's own definition of it as knowing God and the one he sent. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer 'life of the age to come'.

text.q: And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and the one you sent, Jesus Christ.
I glorified you on the earth by completing the work you have given me to do.
And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory I had in your presence before the world existed.
I revealed your name to the people you gave me out of the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

verse.note: In biblical idiom a person's name stands for who that person is: character, identity and authority. To reveal God's name is to make God himself known, not merely to disclose a title. Some interpreters also hear an allusion to the divine name of Exodus 3, but that is debated.

text.q: Now they have come to know that everything you have given me is from you,
because the words you gave me I have given to them, and they received them and came to know in truth that I came from you, and they believed that you sent me.
I am asking on their behalf. I am not asking on behalf of the world but on behalf of those you have given me, because they are yours,

verse.note: Older translations have 'I pray for them'. The verb is the everyday word for asking or making a request, and this Gospel does not use the usual Greek verb for praying at all. Many modern translations likewise render it 'ask'.

text.q: and all that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them.
I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, so that they may be one just as we are.

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mean 'in' (kept within the sphere of what God's name stands for) or 'by' (protected by the power of that name). Translations divide between the two, and the same question arises in verse 12.

note.traditional: those whom thou hast given me

verse.note: The earliest and best manuscripts read 'your name, which you have given me', so that what is given is the name. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'those whom you have given me', making the disciples what is given. Modern editions and most modern translations follow the earlier reading here and in verse 12.

text.q: While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I guarded them, and not one of them was lost except the son of destruction, so that the scripture might be fulfilled.

verse.note: 'Son of' is a Semitic idiom for someone who belongs to or is destined for a thing. In Greek the noun shares its root with the verb just translated 'was lost', so the phrase says in effect that the only one lost was the one who belonged to loss. Judas is meant, and the scripture in view is usually taken to be Psalm 41:9, quoted at John 13:18.

text.q: But now I am coming to you, and I am saying these things in the world so that they may have my joy made full in themselves.
I have given them your word, and the world has hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.
I am not asking that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.

verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine ('the evil one', the devil) or neuter ('evil' in general). Most modern translations and commentators choose the personal sense, in line with this Gospel's references to 'the ruler of this world' and with 1 John 5:18–19. The King James Version has 'the evil'.

text.q: They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.
Consecrate them in the truth; your word is truth.

verse.note: The traditional 'sanctify' now suggests gradual moral improvement. In the Greek Old Testament this verb is used for setting people and offerings apart for God's service, such as priests, prophets and sacrifices. That is the sense in verse 19, where Jesus consecrates himself. The verb is related to 'holy' in the address 'Holy Father' in verse 11; several modern translations also use 'consecrate' here.

text.q: Just as you sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world.
And for their sake I consecrate myself, so that they too may be consecrated in truth.
I am not asking on behalf of these only, but also on behalf of those who believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'that they also may be one in us'. Important early manuscripts lack the word 'one' here, and most modern editions regard it as a copyist's addition echoing the opening of the verse.

text.q: The glory you have given me I have given to them, so that they may be one just as we are one,
I in them and you in me, so that they may be made completely one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them just as you loved me.
Father, I want those you have given me to be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.
Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have come to know that you sent me.
I made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

verse.text: After saying these things, Jesus went out with his disciples across the Kidron ravine, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered.
Now Judas, who was handing him over, also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples.
verse.note: The Greek verb means ‘hand over’ or ‘deliver up’ and is the same one used in verses 30, 35 and 36 for the authorities handing Jesus over to Pilate. Most translations use ‘betray’ when Judas is the subject, and betrayal is certainly what the act amounts to, but the verb itself does not say so; Greek has a separate word for a traitor. Keeping one English verb lets the reader see the chain of handings-over that John traces through the chapter.

verse.text: So Judas took the cohort, along with officers from the chief priests and from the Pharisees, and came there with lanterns and torches and weapons.

note.traditional: a band of men; a detachment of soldiers

verse.note: This is the regular Greek term for a Roman cohort, a unit of auxiliary troops nominally about six hundred strong, though the word could also be used of a smaller detachment. John need not mean that the whole unit turned out. The ‘commander’ in verse 12 translates the Greek title used for a Roman military tribune, the officer in charge of a cohort. John thus presents Roman soldiers and the temple authorities’ own officers as acting together in the arrest.

verse.text: Then Jesus, knowing everything that was coming upon him, went out and said to them, “Who are you looking for?”
They answered him, “Jesus of Nazareth.” He said to them, “I am he.” And Judas, who was handing him over, was standing there with them.
verse.note: The Greek is simply ‘I am’ (ego eimi). In ordinary speech this is how one says ‘That’s me’, and that is its surface meaning here. It is also the phrase with which God speaks in the Greek version of Isaiah, and which Jesus uses without a predicate earlier in John (8:58). The reaction in verse 6 suggests John intends the reader to hear both; some translations print ‘I AM’ to bring out the second sense.

verse.text: So when he said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.
So he asked them again, “Who are you looking for?” And they said, “Jesus of Nazareth.”
Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. So if it is me you are looking for, let these men go.”
This was to fulfill the word he had spoken: “Of those you have given me, I have lost not one.”
Then Simon Peter, who had a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s slave and cut off his right ear. The slave’s name was Malchus.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired employee, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. ‘Servant’ is the older English rendering; several recent translations use ‘slave’. The ‘slave girl’ of verse 17 renders the corresponding feminine term.

verse.text: So Jesus said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup the Father has given me—am I not to drink it?”
So the cohort and its commander and the officers of the Jewish leaders arrested Jesus and bound him
verse.note: The Greek says simply ‘the Jews’, the same word translated that way in verses 20, 33, 35 and 39. In John’s account of the arrest and trial the group in view is plainly the authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole, and it is rendered accordingly here and in verses 14, 31, 36 and 38. Scholars are divided on the word generally: some argue for ‘Judeans’ throughout, while others object that this erases Jews from the New Testament.

verse.text: and led him first to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.
Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jewish leaders that it was better for one man to die for the people.
Simon Peter was following Jesus, and so was another disciple. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he went with Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard,
but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, the one known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the woman who kept the door, and brought Peter in.
Then the slave girl who kept the door said to Peter, “You are not one of this man’s disciples too, are you?” He said, “I am not.”
Now the slaves and the officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing there warming themselves. Peter too was with them, standing and warming himself.
Then the high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.
verse.note: John calls Caiaphas the high priest in verses 13 and 24, yet the questioner here appears to be Annas, since Jesus is sent on to Caiaphas only in verse 24. Annas had held the office from about AD 6 to 15 before being deposed by the Romans; he remained highly influential, and several members of his family held the office after him. Former high priests seem to have kept the title, which is the usual explanation of John’s wording.

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and I said nothing in secret.

text.q: Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Look, they know what I said.”

verse.text: When he said this, one of the officers standing by gave Jesus a slap, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”
Jesus answered him, “If I spoke wrongly, testify to what was wrong; but if rightly, why do you hit me?”
Then Annas sent him, bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.
Meanwhile Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You are not one of his disciples too, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”
One of the high priest’s slaves, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”
So Peter denied it again, and at once a rooster crowed.
Then they led Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the headquarters, so that they would not be defiled but could eat the Passover.

note.term: so that they would not be defiled
