verse.note: Entering a Gentile’s residence was regarded as conveying ritual impurity, which would have barred a person from the Passover meal. In John’s account that meal still lies ahead on this morning, whereas in Matthew, Mark and Luke Jesus has already eaten the Passover with his disciples the evening before. The difference in chronology has long been discussed and is not settled.

verse.text: So Pilate came out to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man were not doing wrong, we would not have handed him over to you.”
So Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Jewish leaders said to him, “We are not permitted to put anyone to death.”

note.term: We are not permitted to put anyone to death
note.traditional: It is not lawful for us to put any man to death

verse.note: In Roman provinces the power to execute was generally reserved to the governor. How strictly this applied in Judea is debated by historians, but John’s statement fits the general pattern. For John the point is the one made in verse 32: a Roman execution meant crucifixion, the ‘lifting up’ that Jesus had spoken of (12:32–33).

verse.text: This was to fulfill the word Jesus had spoken, indicating what kind of death he was going to die.
So Pilate went back into the headquarters, summoned Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”
Jesus answered, “Are you saying this on your own, or did others tell you about me?”
Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?”
verse.note: This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually translated ‘Gentiles’ in this translation. Here, in the singular and in the mouth of a Roman, it means the Jewish people as a nation.

verse.text: Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not from this world. If my kingdom were from this world, my officers would be fighting so that I would not be handed over to the Jewish leaders. But as it is, my kingdom is not from here.”
verse.note: The Greek preposition states source or origin, as the closing words of the verse, ‘not from here’, confirm. The traditional ‘not of this world’ is easily heard as ‘otherworldly’ or ‘having nothing to do with this world’, which is not what the Greek says. The statement is about where Jesus’s kingship comes from and therefore how it operates, not about where it applies; some modern translations already use ‘from’.

The Greek word is the one used in verses 3, 12, 18 and 22 for the officers sent by the chief priests, and it means someone who carries out a superior’s orders. Most translations switch to ‘servants’ or ‘followers’ here. Keeping the same English word preserves John’s contrast between the officers who arrested Jesus and the officers Jesus says would be fighting for him if his kingdom were of that kind.

verse.text: So Pilate said to him, “So you are a king, then?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I have come into the world: to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.”

note.term: You say that I am a king
note.traditional: Thou sayest that I am a king

verse.note: The reply can be read as non-committal (‘king is your word’), as an affirmation (‘you are right to say that I am a king’), or, taking the Greek conjunction as ‘because’, as ‘You say so, because I am a king’. Most interpreters take it as a qualified acceptance: Jesus does not deny the title but goes on to define his purpose in terms of testifying to the truth. The rendering here leaves the reply as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” Having said this, he went out again to the Jewish leaders and said to them, “I find no grounds for a charge against him.

text.q: But you have a custom that I release someone to you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”

verse.text: So they shouted back, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a bandit.
verse.note: The Greek word means an armed brigand who uses violence, not a thief. The Jewish historian Josephus uses it regularly for insurgents against Rome, and Mark and Luke connect Barabbas with an uprising and with murder. Some translations therefore render it ‘insurrectionist’ or paraphrase accordingly; ‘bandit’ keeps the word’s ordinary sense while allowing that overtone.

verse.text: Then Pilate took Jesus and had him flogged.
And the soldiers wove a crown out of thorns and put it on his head, and they wrapped a purple robe around him,
and they kept coming up to him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and slapping him in the face.
Pilate went outside again and said to them, “Look, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no grounds for a charge against him.”
So Jesus came outside, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. And Pilate said to them, “Here is the man!”
When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted, “Crucify! Crucify!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no grounds for a charge against him.”
The Jewish leaders answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die, because he made himself Son of God.”
verse.note: The Greek says simply 'the Jews', and most translations keep that. In this trial scene the group pressing Pilate is the Jerusalem authorities (the chief priests and their officers of verse 6), not the Jewish people as a whole, so the narrower rendering is used here and in verses 12, 14, 31 and 38. Scholars are divided on how to translate the word: some argue for 'Judeans' throughout, others object that this erases Jews from the New Testament.

verse.text: When Pilate heard this statement, he became even more afraid,
and he went back into the governor’s headquarters and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.
So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”
Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all if it had not been given to you from above. For this reason the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”
From then on Pilate tried to release him, but the Jewish leaders shouted, “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Everyone who makes himself king opposes Caesar.”
verse.note: 'Friend of Caesar' was a recognised term for someone who enjoyed the emperor's favour, and losing that standing could end a career or worse. Whether Pilate held it as a formal title is uncertain. Either way, the threat is that releasing a self-declared king would be reported to Rome as disloyalty.

verse.text: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat down on the judge’s seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, or in Hebrew, Gabbatha.
verse.note: The Greek verb can also mean 'seated (someone)', so the sentence could say that Pilate seated Jesus on the judge's seat, as a mocking presentation of him as king. A minority of scholars read it that way. Most take it as Pilate himself sitting to give judgment, which is the usual sense of this verb form in the New Testament.

The Greek word means 'in the language of the Hebrews'. Gabbatha and Golgotha (verse 17) are Aramaic in form, and Greek writers of the period did not always distinguish Hebrew from Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Palestine. For that reason many modern translations render 'in Aramaic' here.

verse.text: Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jewish leaders, “Here is your king!”

note.term: the day of Preparation of the Passover

verse.note: 'Preparation' was the ordinary name for Friday, the day on which preparations were made for the Sabbath. The phrase can therefore mean 'the Friday of Passover week' or 'the day of preparing for the Passover meal'. The choice bears on whether John dates the crucifixion to the day before Passover began, and the question is disputed.

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon. Mark 15:25 places the crucifixion at the third hour, and the difference has long been discussed without an agreed solution. Some interpreters think John's timing is meant to recall the hour when the slaughter of the Passover lambs began.

verse.text: They shouted, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”
Then he handed him over to them to be crucified. So they took charge of Jesus.
And carrying the cross himself, he went out to what is called the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha,
where they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, with Jesus in the middle.
Pilate also wrote a notice and put it on the cross. It read: “Jesus the Nazarene, the King of the Jews.”
Many of the Jews read this notice, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write ‘The King of the Jews,’ but that this man said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his clothes and divided them into four shares, a share for each soldier, and they took the tunic as well. Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top in one piece throughout.

So they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to see whose it will be.” This was so that the scripture would be fulfilled that says, “They divided my clothes among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So that is what the soldiers did.
Now standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

note.term: his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene
note.traditional: his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene

verse.note: The Greek can be read as naming four women, with the mother's sister unnamed, or three, with 'Mary of Clopas' being the sister. Most scholars count four, partly because two sisters both named Mary would be unusual. The Greek says only 'Mary of Clopas'; 'wife' is the most likely relationship, but daughter or mother is possible.

verse.text: When Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.”
verse.note: In Greek this was a normal and courteous way to address a woman, without the coldness the word carries in English. Jesus addresses other women the same way in this Gospel. It is nonetheless an unusual way for a son to address his mother, and interpreters differ on what it implies.

verse.text: Then he said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.
After this, knowing that everything was now finished, and so that the scripture would be completed, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.”
verse.note: John uses his usual word for scripture being 'fulfilled' in verses 24 and 36. Here he uses a different verb, one that shares its root with 'finished' in this verse and in verse 30, and 'completed' keeps that echo. The clause could also attach to what precedes ('everything was now finished so that the scripture would be completed'), but most interpreters link it to Jesus's words 'I am thirsty'.

verse.text: A jar full of sour wine was standing there. So they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop stalk and held it up to his mouth.
verse.note: This was a cheap, sharp wine, usually diluted with water, the everyday drink of soldiers and labourers. Older English versions say 'vinegar', which suggests something undrinkable. It was in fact a common thirst-quencher, and the jar most likely belonged to the soldiers.

verse.text: When Jesus had taken the sour wine, he said, “It is finished.” And he bowed his head and handed over his spirit.
verse.note: The verb is the same one used in this chapter for Jesus being 'handed over' to Pilate and to crucifixion (verses 11 and 16), and the rendering keeps that repetition. It presents Jesus's death as his own deliberate act. Some interpreters also see a hint of the giving of the Spirit, since the Greek says literally 'the spirit', but most take the phrase simply as a description of his death.

verse.text: Since it was the day of Preparation, the Jewish leaders did not want the bodies to remain on the crosses during the Sabbath, for that Sabbath was a great day. So they asked Pilate to have their legs broken and the bodies taken away.
So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man, and then of the other who had been crucified with him.
But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs,
but one of the soldiers stabbed his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
The one who saw it has testified, and his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.
verse.note: The Greek says 'that one knows', and it is not certain who 'that one' is. Most take it as the eyewitness himself, usually identified with the disciple whom Jesus loved. Others think the writer is appealing to a second party, either the witness as distinct from the writer, or Christ or God as guarantor of the testimony.

verse.text: For these things happened so that the scripture would be fulfilled: “Not a bone of his will be broken.”

note.term: “Not a bone of his will be broken.”
note.traditional: A bone of him shall not be broken

verse.note: The wording is closest to the rule for the Passover lamb, whose bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). It also resembles Psalm 34:20, about God guarding the bones of the righteous. Many scholars think John has both in view, presenting Jesus as the Passover lamb and as the righteous sufferer.

verse.text: And again, another scripture says, “They will look on the one they pierced.”

After this, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, though a secret one for fear of the Jewish leaders, asked Pilate to let him take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave permission. So he came and took away his body.
Nicodemus also came, the one who had first come to him by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes weighing about a hundred pounds.
verse.note: The unit is the Roman pound, about 327 grams, so the total is roughly 33 kilograms, or about 72 modern pounds. This is a very large and costly quantity of spices, on the scale of a royal burial.

verse.text: So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.
So, because it was the day of Preparation of the Jews and the tomb was close by, they laid Jesus there.
Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb.
So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple, the one Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have put him.”
So Peter and the other disciple set out and were going to the tomb.
The two were running together, but the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and came to the tomb first,
and bending down to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.
Then Simon Peter also came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
and the face cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up separately, in a place of its own.
Then the other disciple, who had come to the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
verse.note: The Greek does not say what the disciple believed. Most interpreters take it as the first faith that Jesus had risen, with the next verse explaining that this faith came from what he saw and not yet from an understanding of Scripture. A minority view, found already in antiquity, is that he simply believed Mary's report that the body was gone.

verse.text: for they did not yet understand the scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
So the disciples went back again to their homes.
But Mary stood outside by the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had been lying, one at the head and one at the feet.
They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have put him.”
Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?” Supposing that he was the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him off, tell me where you have put him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabbouni!” (which means Teacher).
verse.note: The Greek word means 'in the language of the Hebrews' and was used in this period without distinguishing Hebrew from Aramaic, the related language most Jews of Judea and Galilee spoke every day. 'Rabbouni' is an Aramaic form, so 'in Aramaic' is used here. Older translations and some current ones have 'in Hebrew'; others make the same choice as this one. Jesus also addresses Mary by the Semitic form of her name, Mariam.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God.’”

note.term: Do not hold on to me

verse.note: The verb can mean either 'touch' or 'take hold of, cling to'. The form of the command used here often means 'stop doing' something already under way. Most modern translations therefore have 'do not hold on to me' or 'do not cling to me' in place of the older 'touch me not'. The sense is that Mary must not try to keep him as he was, since he is on his way to the Father. How the reason given ('for I have not yet ascended') fits the command remains debated.

verse.text: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord,” and that he had said these things to her.

When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were locked where the disciples were, for fear of the Jewish leaders, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'the Jews'. The disciples behind the locked doors are themselves Jews, so the word here refers to the Jerusalem authorities who had brought about Jesus's execution, as it often does in John. Scholars are divided on how to render the term in this Gospel: some keep 'the Jews' throughout, and others prefer 'Judeans'.

verse.text: Having said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
So Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I am sending you.”
Having said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathes the breath of life into the first human (Genesis 2:7) and when breath enters the slain in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). A reader who knew those passages would hear an act of new creation. The Greek word for 'Spirit' also means 'breath'.

text.q: If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven them; if you retain anyone’s, they are retained.”

verse.note: The verbs 'are forgiven' and 'are retained' are in the Greek perfect tense, which describes a settled state. Some take this to mean 'they have already been forgiven', so that the disciples declare what God has done; most read it as stating the standing result of the disciples' act. The grammar alone does not decide the question, and the verse has been understood differently across Christian traditions.

verse.text: But Thomas, one of the Twelve, the one called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verse.note: Didymos is the ordinary Greek word for 'twin', and a Greek reader would have heard it as a meaning and not as a foreign name. 'Thomas' itself reflects the Aramaic word for 'twin', so John is translating the name for his readers. Translations are divided between 'Didymus' and 'the Twin'.

verse.text: So the other disciples kept telling him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger into the mark of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will never believe.”
Eight days later his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Though the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
verse.note: Ancient counting usually included both the first and the last day. 'After eight days' therefore means a week later, on the following first day of the week.

verse.text: Then he said to Thomas, “Bring your finger here and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side. Do not be unbelieving, but believing.”

note.term: Do not be unbelieving, but believing

verse.note: The Greek sets two matching adjectives side by side, apistos and pistos, 'unbelieving' and 'believing', and the rendering keeps the pair. Several modern translations have 'do not doubt but believe' or 'stop doubting and believe', which is the source of the phrase 'doubting Thomas'. The Greek has no word for doubt here; Thomas had flatly refused to believe (verse 25).

verse.text: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

note.term: Have you believed because you have seen me?
note.traditional: Because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, so the words can be read as a question or as a statement ('Because you have seen me, you have believed'). The edition translated here punctuates it as a question, as do several modern translations. Either way the remark is a mild contrast with those who believe without seeing, not a rejection of Thomas's confession.

verse.text: Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and so that by believing you may have life in his name.
verse.note: The manuscripts differ by one letter between two forms of the verb. One naturally suggests 'may go on believing' and the other 'may come to believe'. The edition translated here prints the first. The choice bears on whether the Gospel was written mainly to strengthen believers or to win new ones, though many scholars doubt the verb form alone can settle that.

The Greek christos is here a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and the claim is that Jesus is that figure. 'Messiah', from the Hebrew equivalent, conveys the title to a modern reader, for whom 'Christ' sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in passages like this while keeping 'Christ' where it functions as a name.

verse.text: After this Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.
verse.note: This is the lake more often called the Sea of Galilee. The name comes from the city of Tiberias on its western shore, founded by Herod Antipas and named for the emperor Tiberius.

verse.text: Simon Peter, Thomas who was called the Twin, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.” They said to him, “We are coming with you too.” They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing.
When dawn was already breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; the disciples, however, did not know that it was Jesus.
So Jesus said to them, “Children, you don’t have any fish, do you?” They answered him, “No.”
He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and they were no longer able to haul it in because of the great number of fish.

So that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he tied his outer garment around him, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean completely unclothed, but in ordinary usage it also described someone wearing only an undergarment or loincloth, as a labourer would. Most scholars think Peter was lightly clad for fishing and tucked or tied on his outer garment before going to meet Jesus. Some hold instead that he was wearing only a smock, which he belted up in order to swim.

verse.text: But the other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from land, only about two hundred cubits away.
verse.note: A cubit was the length of a forearm, roughly 45 centimetres or 18 inches. Two hundred cubits is about ninety metres, or a hundred yards.

verse.text: When they got out onto the land, they saw a charcoal fire laid there, with fish lying on it, and bread.
verse.note: This word occurs in only one other place in the New Testament: the charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter stood when he denied Jesus three times (John 18:18). Many interpreters think the echo is deliberate, setting the scene for the threefold question that follows.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.”
So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net to land, full of large fish, a hundred and fifty-three of them; and although there were so many, the net was not torn.

note.traditional: an hundred and fifty and three

verse.note: Since antiquity readers have proposed symbolic meanings for this number, but no explanation has won general agreement. It may simply be an eyewitness detail, since fishermen counted a catch in order to divide it.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Come, have breakfast.” None of the disciples dared to ask him, “Who are you?” for they knew it was the Lord.
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and likewise the fish.
This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to the disciples after being raised from the dead.
When they had eaten breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
verse.note: The Greek can mean 'more than these other disciples love me', 'more than you love these men', or 'more than you love these things', meaning the boat and nets. Most interpreters take the first sense, recalling Peter's earlier claim to outdo the others in loyalty. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek does.

Jesus' first two questions use the verb agapaō and his third uses phileō, while Peter answers with phileō each time. An older and still popular reading sees a contrast between a higher love and mere affection. Most current scholars judge the change to be stylistic, since this Gospel uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere, and the passage also varies its words for 'know', 'feed' and 'sheep' without a clear difference in meaning. Both verbs are therefore rendered 'love'.

verse.text: He said to him again, a second time, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Shepherd my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved that he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were younger, you used to fasten your own belt and walk wherever you wanted; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will fasten your belt and carry you where you do not want to go.”

verse.note: The next verse says that this saying points to the manner of Peter's death. Ancient writers used the stretching out of the hands as an expression for crucifixion, and early Christian tradition held that Peter was crucified in Rome. Most interpreters read the phrase in that light, though the image taken by itself could describe a helpless old man being dressed and led.

verse.text: He said this to indicate by what kind of death Peter would glorify God. And after saying this, he said to him, “Follow me.”
Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following, the one who had also leaned back against his chest at the supper and said, “Lord, who is the one handing you over?”
verse.note: The verb means to hand over or deliver up. It is the ordinary word for delivering someone into custody, and it does not by itself carry the sense of treachery that 'betray' does. The traditional rendering is 'betray', which fits what Judas did but adds a colouring the Greek word leaves to the context.

verse.text: So when Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, and what about this man?”
Jesus said to him, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”

So this saying went out among the brothers and sisters, that that disciple would not die. Yet Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?”
verse.note: The Greek plural, traditionally 'brothers' or 'brethren', was the normal way to refer to a mixed group of siblings. Here it means the community of believers, women as well as men.

verse.text: This is the disciple who is testifying about these things and who wrote these things, and we know that his testimony is true.
verse.note: The shift to 'we' and then to 'I' in the next verse has led most scholars to conclude that these closing lines, and perhaps the whole chapter, were added by members of the beloved disciple's circle, who vouch for his testimony. Others take the 'we' as the author's own manner of speaking. No surviving manuscript of the Gospel lacks this chapter.

verse.text: But there are also many other things that Jesus did; if every one of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have room for the books that would be written.
